activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: One Vindolanda tablet is a birthday party invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, written around 100 CE, with closing lines that are among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.
story:
The reading room of the county archive smelled of paper dust and radiator oil, and Laurence had claimed the corner table before anyone else arrived because she needed, this week, to prove a point. Her history teacher, Ms. Nasser, had assigned a short essay on Roman Britain and had refused to tell them what to argue. "Find a question you actually want answered," she had said, which Laurence found both thrilling and useless, like being handed a map with the roads left off. Her question, chosen Sunday night and defended to herself since, was this: what did ordinary women on the frontier actually say to each other? Her working answer, typed at the top of her notes, was "nothing that survived," and she intended to write a ferocious paragraph about erasure.

Isabella slid into the chair beside her with a thermos and no notebook, which was Isabella's way of announcing that she was here for company and not for labour. Sidney arrived eleven minutes later, dropped his bag, and immediately began describing a documentary about gladiators that Laurence suspected was tangential at best, though he swore it was research.

"Nobody wrote letters," she said, cutting him off. "Not women. Not ordinary ones. papyrus rots, wood rots, everything rots, so we get generals and emperors and men complaining about grain shipments. That's the whole record."

"That's a grim essay," Sidney said.

"It's an honest essay." She had spent a term's worth of resentment on it, the feeling that every unit of history class had been men deciding things while women stood in the margins like furniture. She wanted to say that out loud, in academic prose, with citations.

Ms. Nasser appeared behind them with a box of facsimiles the archive kept for school visits, the folded replicas of wooden tablets excavated from a fort in the north of England. "Vindolanda," she said, and set the box down. "Don't touch the originals in the case. These you can handle." Then she moved off toward the front desk, offering nothing further, which was her method and her cruelty.

Laurence pulled the first facsimile out expecting accounts, and the second expecting requisitions, and the third was a birthday invitation. She read the transcription card twice. Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, greeting her friend, asking her to come to her sister's birthday celebration on the eleventh, promising to make the day more delightful for her company, and then, in the closing lines, added in a different hand, a warm personal note to her dearest friend. Around 100 CE, the card said, and those closing lines were thought to be among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman, possibly written by Claudia herself.

"It's like a birthday card," Isabella said, looking over her shoulder. "It's literally a birthday card."

"Sister, my dearest soul," Laurence read aloud, her voice doing something embarrassing in the middle, "I hoped that I might see you, but I was not allowed." She set the tablet down carefully on the felt mat. Two women on the edge of the empire, one of them asking the other to a party, the other adding her own hand, and it had survived because the mud had preserved the wood instead of destroying it. Her ferocious paragraph about erasure was suddenly, quietly, wrong, or at least not wholly right.

Sidney leaned in. "So there's one letter. One. Out of how many?"

"That's the problem," Laurence said. "There's one, so my essay that says there's nothing is false. But one invitation doesn't tell me what their lives were like either. Maybe thousands of letters existed and this is the accident that survived. Maybe Claudia was unusual, a commander's wife with scribes and leisure, and the women I actually wanted are still silent." She turned the facsimile over. "Ms. Nasser said historians fight about these tablets all the time. I thought historians fought because someone was wrong. But it's more like they're all holding different torches in the same dark room."

"Write that down," Isabella said. "That's better than your essay."

Laurence laughed despite herself, then didn't, because she was already writing. She crossed out her old opening line and sat staring at the blank space where it had been. She could write, she decided, about the invitation and about the silence around it at the same time, holding both, admitting where the evidence stopped. It felt like an armistice between the two essays she had wanted to write, though she suspected it was the harder one.

"What's the question now?" Sidney asked, chin on his hand.

Laurence looked at the card again, at the line about not being allowed to come, and began to write at the top of the page: What can one birthday invitation prove, and what can it not?

"I hope my girl is in good health," she said, reading the last line out loud, almost to herself. "I think she is."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down and sparks at roughly 3 million volts per metre, which limits how strong a field can be across an air gap.
story:
The skate park was quiescent at nine in the morning, the concrete still cool, everything smelling faintly of rain that had never arrived, and Aidan had the best bench to himself with his physics worksheet flat on his knee. Farhan arrived with his board under his arm and a bag of day-old doughnuts, which he traded, half a chocolate glazed for one answered question, an arrangement Aidan privately considered the most successful mutualism in his life, since he could not ollie and Farhan could not compute.

"Question four," Aidan said. "Two plates, three millimetres apart, nine thousand volts across them. Field strength in between."

"Divide the big scary number by the small boring number," Farhan said, mouth full. "You told me that twice."

Aidan wrote it out. Nine thousand volts over three thousandths of a metre, which came to three million volts per metre. He underlined it, twice, the way he did when an answer came out round, because round answers felt like the universe winking at you.

"Done," he said. "Three million volts per metre. Beautiful."

Farhan leaned over his shoulder, squinting at the underline. "Three million volts per metre," he repeated. "Hang on. Is that not the number where the air just gives up?"

"Gives up how?"

"Dude. Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down and sparks at roughly three million volts per metre. That's the limit. You can't get a stronger field than that across an air gap. It just goes crack."

Aidan looked at his underlined answer, which had gone from beautiful to ominous in one sentence. "Where do you even know that from?"

"My uncle does laser stuff in a lab. He disabused me of the idea that you can just crank voltage forever. There was a demonstration. There was a smell." Farhan mimed a small explosion between two palms. "So either your worksheet wants the air to spark, or you did it wrong."

"Or the worksheet is a trap," Aidan said slowly, and this possibility delighted him so much he almost forgave the worksheet its other three questions. Because if the plates were three millimetres apart in air, and the field between them was exactly three million volts per metre, then the problem wasn't asking for a number at all. It was asking whether the setup could exist. The ceiling wasn't decoration; it was the whole point. Any more voltage across that gap and the air itself would give up its polite silence and go crack, and the plates would discharge and the field would collapse. The question had been sitting there disguised as arithmetic.

Ms. Chan came through the gate then, walking the small opinionated dog from three doors down, the way she did every morning. She taught at the college and had a habit of stopping at Aidan's bench to inspect his work without asking, which he pretended to resent and did not.

"Three millimetres," she read off his page. "Nine thousand volts."

"Three million volts per metre," Aidan said. "Which is where air sparks, so the field's right at the limit, so the answer is yes, barely, and it's kind of a nasty question."

She looked at him for a second longer than usual. "Last week you told me physics was just plugging in numbers."

"I was young then," Aidan said, and Farhan made a choking noise into his doughnut.

Ms. Chan unclipped the dog's leash so it could investigate a chip bag with terrible commitment, and sat down on the end of the bench. She did not explain anything, which Aidan appreciated. Instead she asked what happened at four millimetres, and he worked it: nine thousand over four thousandths, two and a quarter million, comfortably under the ceiling. And then, unprompted, what voltage would sit right at the ceiling for four millimetres, and he got twelve million, wait, no, twelve thousand, and Farhan said "same energy" and both of them laughed at the idea of a twelve-million-volt classroom demo.

"Here's what I still don't know," Aidan said, tapping the worksheet. "Whether the air sparking makes the setup useless or makes it interesting. Like, is the limit a wall or a door?"

"That," said Ms. Chan, standing and re-clipping the dog, "is the correct question to bring to college in two years." She left him with that, and Farhan stole the last doughnut as tax.

Aidan copied his answer into the margin, then added one line beneath it: air quits at three million, and folded the page into his back pocket. Farhan dropped his board on the concrete and pushed off toward the shallow bowl, and after a moment Aidan left the bench and ran after him, worksheet crinkling against his hip the whole way down.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: JUnit's assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second, so swapping them gives confusing failure messages.
story:
The kitchen table had been Henry's father's workbench for the evening, cleared of placemats and colonized by a laptop, a spiral notebook, and two mugs of tea going cold at different rates. He was building a BankAccount class, private fields, getters, the whole architecture Mr. Shapiro had sketched on the board that morning in green marker that squeaked. Henry had gotten the class itself done in an hour. The test file was defeating him.

The failure message on his screen read, in red, that the test expected thirty when the method returned fifty. He stared at it the way you stare at a door that has always opened inward and now, apparently, opens outward. He had written the withdrawal method with fifty as the starting balance and thirty as the amount to subtract. He had written the test line in the same order, thinking the numbers would land in their natural places. Somewhere between his file and the red message, they had swapped allegiances.

Delaney was sprawled on the living room floor with her own laptop, ostensibly doing her English reading, actually watching him fail in the reflective dark of her screen. She got up when he swore, quietly, at the refrigerator's hum.

"Show me," she said, dragging a chair around beside his. She read the test line aloud, one finger under it on the screen. "You put fifty second. That's the actual value, right? What the method gives back."

"I don't know what it is. That's the problem. I wrote it the way I thought of it. Fifty starts, thirty leaves."

"Try switching them," she said. "Just to see what the message does. Not because it's right."

He cut the thirty, pasted it into the first position, moved the fifty second, and ran the test again. The red message transformed itself. Now it said the test expected fifty and got fifty, and a green bar appeared where the red one had been, and Delaney made a small noise through her teeth like a person watching a tightrope walker land.

"So it's the expected value first," Henry said slowly, writing it in the notebook. "Then the actual. The thing you want, then the thing you got."

"That's going to confuse you again," Delaney said. "You'll write it your way every time and be shocked every time."

He was quiet for a second, because she was right about a larger thing than the test. All year he had been treating the class as a place where the machine should meet him where he stood, and all year the machine had declined, politely and inflexibly. His father passed through with the mail and stopped, reading the green bar upside down.

"Fixed it?" his father asked.

"Turned the numbers around," Henry said. "The order matters. I had it backwards."

His father nodded and set an orange by Henry's elbow without comment, which was his way of saying he was glad the boy was at the table doing something instead of upstairs scrolling himself into a disaffected trance, a phrase Henry had overheard in February and resented at the time. Now, with the green bar glowing, he could admit the description had been accurate for most of that winter. He peeled the orange and offered Delaney a segment, and she took two.

They kept going because Mohammad was coming at seven to work through the same assignment, and Mohammad had missed two weeks with the flu and was terrified in the specific way of a person who fears that everyone else has learned a secret language. Henry began building a second test from scratch, a deposit method this time, and he deliberately wrote the assertion in his natural order, fifty first, thirty second, just to watch the failure message appear again. It did. Expected thirty, actual fifty. He switched them. Green.

"Why would you do that on purpose?" Delaney asked.

"Because if I only see it work, I'll forget. If I see it fail the way I fail, I'll remember the shape of the failure." He pulled the notebook closer and wrote: expected first, actual second, and underlined it twice, and then, after a pause, did not underline it a third time. Some things deserved two underlines and a margin of doubt. It had worked twice. Twice was not a law.

The doorbell rang at six fifty-eight and Mohammad came in holding his laptop like a casserole, and Henry slid over to make room and turned his screen so the green bar faced the doorway. He didn't explain anything yet. He just said, "Before you run anything, write one line exactly backwards on purpose and look at what it tells you."

Mohammad sat down, opened his files, and typed the assertion with the numbers in his own order, the human order, and pressed run.

"Okay," Mohammad said, watching the red bloom across his screen. "That's the most useful wrong thing I've seen all week."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
Rose had signed up for the community studio's open hours because Ms. Nakamura had said, at the last minute of the last class of junior year, that anyone who wanted the good drawing table by the window should come early in September. Rose had not known what she wanted from the studio yet, only that she wanted a place that was not school and not home, a room where she was nobody's daughter and nobody's student, and so on the first Tuesday she arrived at four with a sandwich in her bag and a sketchbook full of portraits she was already half ashamed of.

Giuliano was already at the good table, which was annoying, but he moved his backpack without being asked and made room. He was drawing a bicycle chained to a fence outside, working fast, his hand skating over the page. Samara came in twenty minutes later, shook rain off her jacket, and leaned over Rose's shoulder to look at the portrait Rose had started from a photo on her phone, her grandmother at the kitchen table, taken the summer before the grandmother moved into the home.

"Your shading's smeared everywhere," Samara said. "It looks like the whole face is behind fog."

Rose looked. It was true. She had blended the cheek into shadow and the shadow into the table, and the graphite had traveled, a gray bloom across half the page, so that her grandmother appeared to be dissolving into her own kitchen. Rose turned the pencil in her fingers. On the barrel, small and gold, it said 6B.

Giuliano leaned across. "Which grade did you use?" When she showed him, he nodded as if this confirmed something. "A pencil's core is graphite mixed with clay," he said. "More clay makes it harder, lighter, marked H. Less clay, soft and dark, marked B. That's a 6B, that's basically charcoal pretending to be a pencil." He went back to his bicycle. Rose sat with that for a moment, turning the pencil again, thinking of how she had chosen it because the dark came easily, and how the ease was exactly the problem, how the softness that gave her the shadows she loved also let them wander.

She borrowed an HB from Giuliano's tin and started again on a fresh page. The marks were paler, more stubborn; she had to go over the temple three times to get any depth at all. But when she dragged her finger across a finished passage, testing, almost nothing moved. It occurred to her that there was a whole system here, an alphabet of hardness running along the barrels, and that nobody had ever told her, and that she had been choosing her tools the way she chose most things, by feel, by which one made the first stroke look impressive. She wondered what else she had chosen that way. The thought was uncomfortable enough that she decided to keep drawing.

On Thursday she came back and worked for two hours on the new version, harder pencils for the architecture of the face, the one soft 4B saved for the eyes alone, where she wanted the darkness to live. Ms. Nakamura circulated with her coffee and paused behind Rose long enough to say, "You've been reading the barrels," and Rose said, "Giuliano told me," and Ms. Nakamura said only, "Good," and moved on, which felt like the highest praise available in that room.

That night, unable to sleep, Rose wrote a message to Samara, the kind she would never send:

"I keep thinking about the clay thing. More clay, harder pencil, lighter line, and it's the light line that stays put. The 6B was beautiful in the first minute and gone by the tenth. I applied to the environmental program because it sounded like the thing a serious person does, and to the art one because it sounded like the thing a free person does, and I've been treating it like the smudge is proof of feeling. Maybe. Or maybe the smudge is just the smudge and I'm making it mean something. I don't actually know if choosing the harder pencil is wisdom or just fear with better posture. Call me tomorrow?"

She did not send it. She read it twice, decided it was too much, and then sent it anyway at one in the morning, because Samara had once told her that unsent letters were a technocracy of one, a government of yourself by yourself, with no appeals process, and that this was deleterious to a person over time. Samara had been joking, mostly, but the phrase had stuck, and Rose found she wanted a witness, even a sleepy one.

At the studio on Saturday, Rose taped the second portrait to the window light to check it. Her grandmother's face held. The eyes were dark, the rest quiet and firm, and where Rose's finger tested the cheek, the graphite stayed where it had been put. Her phone buzzed on the table. Samara had replied with one line: "Fear with better posture is still posture. Come draw mine next." Rose picked up the 2H and looked over at Samara, who was already pulling her hair off her face and turning sideways to the window.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius (165 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
Santiago's kitchen smelled of scorched garlic and something sweeter underneath, like onions surrendering. Isla stood at the counter with a printed list, seven dinners, each one broken down into grams and prices, because his mother had agreed to teach her the whole system on the condition that Isla do it herself. She had wanted this for months. In September she would be in a residence with a shared kitchen, and the idea of arriving there knowing nothing, of living on cafeteria fries and whatever her roommate abandoned in the fridge, seemed to portend a small but genuine failure, one she could see coming from far away and still not prevent.

"You're chopping like you're afraid of it," Santiago said from the doorway, an orange in one hand.

"I'm chopping like someone whose mother does all the chopping." She squared off the onion and went back to it, slower now. His mother worked a Saturday shift, so it was just the two of them, and a printed page from the USDA website taped to the cabinet that Santiago had found and taped there himself, which surprised her, because he was not the taping-things-to-cabinets type.

The first hour was shopping, done virtually, since they'd already carried the bags home. Isla spread the receipts across the table and built the week: chicken thighs roasted on Sunday, split across Monday and Wednesday; a pot of rice cooked once and reheated; beans; a tray of vegetables that would go into two different sauces so it didn't feel like the same meal wearing different shirts. It was less like cooking and more like architecture. She kept noticing how the plan rewarded a certain cold ascetic thinking, quantities fixed in advance, no romantic wandering through the produce aisle, and she wasn't sure yet whether that discipline was freeing or merely grim.

Then the cooking, which was where everything stopped being tidy. The garlic burned because she'd left it alone to label containers. The chicken sat stubbornly pink near the bone even after the time the recipe promised. And when Thursday's portion of rice came out of the fridge, dense and clumped, she remembered the taped page and went to read it.

"Where's the thermometer thing?" she called.

"Drawer by the stove. The one with the batteries and the dead pens."

The probe was thin as a knitting needle. She slid it into the middle of the rice in the saucepan, watching the number crawl upward on the little screen while the pan hissed. Sixty degrees. Sixty-four. She'd assumed hot was hot, that steam rising meant safe, the way her mother waved a hand over a plate and pronounced it fine. Sixty-nine. Seventy-one. She leaned closer, oddly fascinated, as though the grains were keeping a secret she could only hear through glass.

"Seventy-four," she said when it held there, then looked back at the page. "Celsius. A hundred sixty-five Fahrenheit. The USDA says reheated leftovers should hit that, all the way through." She pulled the probe out and wiped it on a towel. "That took longer than I thought. Like a full extra minute."

"Congratulations, you have safely reheated rice," Santiago said, and there was something in his voice she caught only sideways, a dryness that didn't quite match his words.

She plated it, added the second sauce, the peanut one, and carried both plates to the table. The food was good. Not transcendent, but hers, planned and executed and reheated to exactly seventy-four degrees Celsius, one hundred sixty-five Fahrenheit, verified by instrument, and she felt a strange pride in the verification itself, in having measured instead of assumed. She told him about the residence kitchen again, how she'd be the person on her floor who actually knew things, and he nodded and peeled another orange and said the peel oil was spraying a noxious mist in her direction, which it wasn't, it smelled like his whole kitchen should have smelled.

It was only when she was washing the pans, sleeves pushed up, that she found the evidence. Taped inside the cabinet above the sink, behind where the kettle sat, a second printout, older, its corners curled: the same USDA page, the same temperature in bold, and beneath it, in Santiago's handwriting from what looked like years ago, "check BEFORE you give any to mom." She stood there with her hands in the cooling water, rearranging the afternoon. The taping-things-to-cabinets type. The drawer where the thermometer already lived among the dead pens, like something that had been used and set down.

"You already knew all of this," she said. "The whole time."

He came over, took the scrubber from her, and turned the tap back to hot. "I knew the number. You learned the week."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A statistically significant result can still be a tiny effect: with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test.
story:
The library had that smell of old carpet and radiator dust, and Katherine had claimed the table by the window before anyone else could, spreading out two photocopies like cards in a hand she didn't yet know how to play. Ms. Demir had assigned the review on Monday: two scholarly articles, same research question, and Katherine had to hold them against each other and decide which one argued better. The question was whether school start times affected student grades. Article A said yes, emphatically. Article B said the evidence was thin. That was all Katherine knew when she sat down, and it felt like being handed two witnesses who disagreed without being allowed to ask either of them anything.

Nicolas dropped into the chair across from her with a granola bar he wasn't supposed to have in the library. "Which one are you going to say is right?" he asked, already unwrapping it.

"That's not the assignment," Katherine said. "It's not about right. It's about which argument holds up." But she noticed, with a small discomfort, that she did want one of them to be right. Article A was cleaner, more confident, and its certainty was seductive in the way a locked door is seductive when you don't have the key. Article B was hedged and careful, full of qualifications that read at first like weakness.

She read Article A again with a pencil, doing what Ms. Demir had told them to do, which was to slow down and check the claims against the numbers. The study had a hundred and eighty thousand students. That was enormous; the whole district, the whole state, maybe. And the finding was that later start times raised grades. The word the authors used was significant, and they used it the way people use the word important, almost as a synonym. "The difference was statistically significant," they wrote, and then they moved on as though the matter were settled.

Katherine almost moved on too. Then she went looking, in the table, for how big the difference actually was, and she sat back in her chair. It was a fraction of a grade point, so small that two students with different start times would look like the same student on a transcript. She looked at the number, then at the word significant, then back at the number. Could both of those be true at once? She turned to Nicolas. "Can something be significant and tiny?"

"Those are opposites," Nicolas said, chewing. "That's basically what significant means. Big."

She pulled Article B toward her and found the passage, the one she'd skimmed past earlier because it seemed fussy. With a very large sample, the article said, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test. A hundred and eighty thousand students. A fraction of a grade point. The pieces clicked together with an almost physical sensation, like a window latch finally catching. Significance was a statement about the test, not about the size of the effect. She read the sentence twice more to be sure she wasn't inventing the conclusion out of her own wish to dismantle Article A, because that was the trap on the other side: wanting the careful article to win just because it was careful.

"You have that face," Nicolas said. "The one where you think you've caught somebody."

"I think I caught myself." She showed him the two numbers side by side, the enormous sample and the tiny difference. "Article A says the finding is significant, and it is, statistically. But when I checked how big the difference actually was, it's nothing you'd notice in a real classroom." She tapped the page. "The big sample is doing the work. That's why they can claim it."

Nicolas frowned at the numbers as if they'd personally deceived him, which in a way they had. "So which article do you say is better?"

"That's the part I can't decide," Katherine said slowly. Article A had the cleaner design and the honest number, and it had still let its language carry more weight than the number could bear. Article B had been right about the trap but was intransigent about everything else, refusing to grant even the modest thing the data did show, as though admitting any effect would be a defeat. She didn't want to write a review that was just casuistry, a clever case dressed up as a judgment. She wanted to say something she actually believed, which was that a tiny real effect was not nothing and not enough, both at once, and she wasn't sure her conclusion could live in the same sentence as both of those clauses. Maybe, she thought, that uncertainty was the honest thing to hand in. Maybe it was just a failure of nerve. She couldn't tell yet which it was, and she suspected no one could tell her.

Ms. Demir passed behind them on her rounds, pausing at the sight of the two articles laid open like a debate in progress. "Finding anything?" she asked, and Katherine, instead of answering, slid Article A across the table and pointed at the word significant.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2018 replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan found the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller, and shrank further after accounting for family background.
story:
Isaac found the letter on the kitchen counter on the first afternoon of spring break, propped against the fruit bowl with his name on it in his grandfather's small, upright hand. The letter said that his grandfather was coming to stay for two weeks while he recovered from his surgery, and that Isaac's mother had volunteered Isaac's room, which meant Isaac would be on the couch in the den. The grandfather arrived that evening with one suitcase and a folding cane he did not yet need, and by the second morning he had installed himself in the armchair by the window, convalescing with the seriousness of a man who believed rest was a discipline rather than a necessity.

They spent the days in a slow orbit around each other. Isaac was supposed to be deciding about college, a decision he had been putting off with a thoroughness that impressed even him. Two schools had accepted him. One was expensive and far away and prestigious in a way people recognized at parties; the other was close and cheap and fine. His mother wanted him to go to the far one and take the loans. "You defer the pleasure now," the grandfather said over lunch on the third day, "and you collect later. That's the whole secret. You know about the marshmallow test?"

Isaac said he had heard of it. Kids given one marshmallow, told they could have two if they waited.

"Exactly. They followed those children up years later, and the ones who waited did better in school, better in life. Character, proven at age four." The grandfather settled back into the chair, pleased with the shape of the argument, as though he had personally administered the test. "So you take the hard road now. You wait. It pays off."

Isaac had been reading late the night before, half avoiding the decision, and he had come across something. He went and got his laptop and found the page again. "There was a redo of it," he said. "A 2018 replication. Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan, and Haonan Quan. They found the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller than the original study said. And after they accounted for family background, it shrank even further." He turned the screen toward the chair.

The grandfather put on his glasses. He read for a long time, his lips moving once or twice, and then he handed the laptop back. "Who are these people?"

"Researchers. It's a real study, not a blog post."

"There's always some dissident with a spreadsheet," the grandfather said. "In my day we called it an excuse." But he said it without much force, and he looked out the window afterward, at the hedge, for most of an hour.

That evening Lilian came by with notes from the physics class Isaac had missed, and the three of them ended up in the kitchen while Isaac made the only dinner he could make, which was pasta with too much garlic. Lilian's family was from a part of the world the grandfather referred to by an old name that no longer existed, and the two of them argued companionably about sectarian politics until Lilian said that in her house, opinions like the grandfather's would have gotten somebody's windows broken, and the grandfather laughed, actually laughed, and told her about a window of his own that had been broken in 1974 for less.

Later, washing dishes, Lilian dried while Isaac told her about the marshmallow study. "He's not wrong that waiting can matter," Isaac said. "If the original study had held up, it would almost be an argument for the expensive school. Suffer now, profit later. But the newer finding makes it messier. If the kids who waited mostly came from steadier families, then what looked like character might have been circumstances. So maybe what I actually have isn't a test of my character. It's a test of what my circumstances can carry." He set a plate in the rack. "Which applies to the loans, actually. My circumstances versus my character. I can't tell them apart from inside."

"So which school?"

"I don't know yet. That's the honest answer."

The grandfather's last night before flying home, they sat up with the television off. The grandfather turned his empty cup in its saucer. "I built my whole life on waiting," he said. "Some of it paid. Some of it I'm still waiting on." He looked at Isaac across the dark room. "The couch suit you?"

"It's fine."

"Good. Decide the school when you decide it. Don't decide it to prove something to me." He stood, took the cane he still did not need, and went down the hall to bed.

Isaac stayed at the table with the two envelopes, which he had taken to carrying in his back pocket like a habit. He took them out and laid them side by side on the wood, the far one and the near one, and left them there while he rinsed the grandfather's cup and set it upside down to dry.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The park had been closed to traffic since dawn, and by noon the lawn behind the boathouse smelled like fried dumplings and burnt string from the firecrackers someone had set off early. Lauren's family claimed a stretch of benches near the willow trees, where her grandmother spread a cloth and began laying out food in the order she always used, noodles first, then the dumplings, then the oranges in a fan. Lauren's cousin arrived with his wife of four months, carrying a thermos and a bag of mandarins, and the aunts rearranged themselves around them, saying how grown-up he looked now.

Lauren had noticed something at last year's dinner and had been thinking about it since. Her grandmother gave out red envelopes, hongbao, stuffed with crisp bills, and last year the cousins who had married received none, while everyone younger got theirs in the usual order, oldest to youngest. Lauren was seventeen now. She had a job at the library, a bank account, a university acceptance letter folded into her backpack. She could not decide which side of the line she was on.

Her friend Regan met her at the edge of the celebration, wearing a red scarf she had bought specifically for the occasion. Carla came too, ebullient as always, taking photographs of the paper lanterns strung between the oak trees and narrating to nobody in particular. "So what's with all the red," Carla asked, zooming in on a banner. "Is it just a color scheme?"

"It's for good fortune," Lauren said. "Keeping bad things away. That's the whole point of it." She pointed at the envelopes her grandmother was counting out of a tin, their red brighter than the scarf, than the banner, than the little flags the children were waving near the stage where a lion dance was about to begin.

They helped at the craft table for a while, where Ms. Chatterjee from the next street was teaching kids to fold paper lanterns with the patience of someone who had done it for thirty years. When the drumming started, they all moved toward the boathouse to watch the lion rear up on its poles, and Lauren lost track of her family in the crowd, then found them again by her grandmother's yellow hat.

The apportionment began after the performance, as it did every year. Her grandmother moved through the younger cousins in strict order, pressing an envelope into each small hand and saying the same words, grow a year, grow in luck. The children ran off immediately to compare amounts, which their parents pretended not to see. Her cousin's wife, who was twenty-six and had received an envelope at this same park the year before, stood with her hands clasped behind her back, and no one offered her one, and she smiled at the ground.

Then her grandmother reached Lauren and paused, and Lauren braced herself, ready to be gracious about it, ready to say she understood, she was practically an adult now. Instead her grandmother took an envelope from her coat pocket, not the tin, a separate one she had apparently carried all day, and pressed it into Lauren's palm and closed her fingers over it.

"You still have time," her grandmother said. "Not married yet."

"Grandma, that's years away. Maybe never."

"Then every year, an envelope." She patted Lauren's hand twice and moved on to her brother.

Lauren stood there holding the envelope, which was stiffer than she expected, probably a larger bill, and she understood that the line she had been trying to locate was not about age at all. It was about something she had never thought to question, a custom that decided for her where she stood in the family, and she found she liked standing there, still counted among the children, still inside the circle of the unmarried young, even as part of her wanted to be past it. Carla appeared at her elbow asking to see, and Regan was saying they should litigate over the last pork bun before the line got long, and somewhere behind them the firecrackers went off in a string of flat reports that scattered the pigeons off the boathouse roof.

"Later," Lauren said, and put the envelope in her inside pocket, the one with the zipper, and got in line behind Regan for the buns.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US National Labor Relations Act, signed on July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively.
story:
The union hall smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and Jonathan stood near the door holding a stack of flyers he had promised to hand out, though he had promised it to himself only, in the parking lot, in the last minute before going in. He was eighteen and had worked at Fetterman's Grocery for eleven months, long enough to know which manager changed the schedule on Fridays and which one docked breaks when the delivery trucks ran late. Tonight the local had opened its hall to grocery workers from three stores, and the folding chairs were filling faster than anyone had planned.

Kellen had come with him, partly out of loyalty and partly because Kellen's mother had been in the nurses' local for twenty years and Kellen considered himself, in his own vernacular, "union born." He took half the flyers without being asked and fanned them like a card dealer. "Look at this," he said. "Half these people are from our store. Nobody told me they cared."

Youssef was already there, sitting in the second row with his jacket still on. He had started at Fetterman's the same week as Jonathan, and he worked the closing shift four nights a week while taking a full course load at the community college. He did not wave. He was watching the man at the podium, a warehouse worker named Mr. Schneider whom Jonathan knew only as the neighbor who fixed his own fence in the rain. Mr. Schneider was not the organizer. He was just a member who had agreed to say a few words.

When Mr. Schneider finished, a woman from the dairy aisle stood up and said what half the room was clearly thinking. "How do we know they can't just fire us for this? Because they can. They fired my cousin at the distribution center for less." A murmur moved through the chairs, and Jonathan felt it pass through him too, because he needed the job. His father was out of work and the house had a mortgage, and eleven months of paychecks were not a theory.

"Okay, but there's a law," Kellen said, standing up anyway, before Jonathan could decide whether to. Kellen had that in him, a readiness to be first. "The National Labor Relations Act," he said. "It gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively." He paused, as though waiting for applause, and got none. "It's from 1935," he added. "July fifth."

Youssef turned around in his chair. "It's true," he said quietly, not to Kellen but to the dairy woman. "I looked it up last night. I wasn't going to come if it was just going to get people fired." He said it the way he said most things, flat and exact, and Jonathan understood that Youssef had done the same reading he had done at two in the morning, and had also not mentioned it to anyone, and had also come anyway.

The dairy woman did not sit down. "So they passed a law in 1935 and that's supposed to protect me in aisle six?" A few people laughed, not kindly, and Mr. Schneider said something from the side of the room about how the law was one thing and enforcement was another, and the organizer in the cardigan asked everyone to split into store groups. The crowd broke apart like something sedimentary, layers sliding along the lines where it had already been divided, store from store, shift from shift, the closers clustering with the closers.

Jonathan's group ended up in the corner by the water fountain. There were nine of them from Fetterman's, including two assistant managers who technically weren't eligible, who had come to listen and stood slightly apart, arms crossed. The organizer handed them a sign-in sheet and said not to put it anywhere the store could see it, and that was the moment the thing stopped being flyers and became a decision. Names on paper. His name on paper.

He thought of his father, who lionized the old strikes the way other men lionized ballplayers, and who also, when Fetterman's cut his department's hours the year before he was laid off, had told Jonathan to keep his head down. Both of those were his father, honestly held, and Jonathan could not make them agree. The law said one thing, July fifth, 1935, a fact he could recite, and the schedule on the wall by the time clock said another thing every Friday. He wrote his name. Beside him, Youssef wrote his without pausing, and then leaned over the sheet and carefully, in small letters, added his hours, as though the paper were a ledger and not a risk.

Kellen signed last, then flipped the pen in his fingers and looked at the door. "You know they'll cut our hours first," he said. "Before anything good happens. That's how it goes." Nobody disagreed. The organizer collected the sheet, folded it, put it inside her jacket, and told them the next meeting was Thursday, same hall. Outside, in the lot, the grocery store's sign glowed half a mile down the road, and Youssef zipped his jacket against the cold and said, "I close tomorrow. If my name's already on that sheet somewhere, I'd kind of like to know before I clock in."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
Dylan had applied to nine places before the coffee shop called him back, which meant he had filled out the phrase "reliable team player" nine times, and by the tenth he no longer believed words meant anything. The shop sat between a laundromat and a shuttered record store, and its owner, Ms. Demetriou, interviewed him at the corner table while a milk steamer screamed behind her like a small appliance in agony.

"You're eighteen," she said, reading his application. "You have no experience."

"I have enthusiasm," Dylan said. "And a bike. The bike is mostly enthusiasm too, honestly."

She hired him anyway, contingent, she said, on two weeks of probation. He signed a form without reading it, which he would later understand was its own kind of answer.

His cousin Rudy lived in Montana, and Rudy called on Dylan's second shift, while Dylan was wiping down the condiment station with the slow, glacial dignity of someone learning that speed comes later.

"Tell your boss she can't fire you," Rudy said, before hello. "You have rights."

"She can fire me for anything. I'm basically a trial-size employee."

"Not here, man. Not in Montana. After the probationary period, my boss actually needs good cause to fire me. It's the one state in the whole country like that. The Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act. Nineteen eighty-seven."

Dylan held the phone away from his ear and looked at it, the way you look at a friend who has just claimed to be able to juggle. "You made that up. That sounds like something you'd make up."

"Look it up," Rudy said. "Alayna's there, right? Make her look it up. She likes being right more than she likes you."

Alayna was in fact there, in the window seat, pretending to study for a statistics final while actually ranking the café's regulars by how badly they treated the baristas. She had known Dylan since seventh grade, when they had bonded over a shared hatred of the word "moist," and she took the phone with the air of a judge accepting a case.

"Montana," she said gravely. "Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act. I'm looking it up." A pause, during which the espresso grinder roared and Dylan restacked napkins that did not need restacking. "Rudy's right. It's real. Montana's the only state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire someone. Nineteen eighty-seven, just like he said."

"Generally," Dylan repeated. "That word is doing a lot of work."

"That word is doing all the work in every law ever written," Alayna said, and passed the phone back.

Dylan carried this around for the rest of his shift like a coin in his shoe. On one side was Rudy's certainty, the idea that a job could be a thing you held onto, that the law underpinned you like a floor you didn't have to think about. On the other side was everything Ms. Demetriou had said during the interview, which had amounted to: you are here until I decide otherwise. Both of them were true in their own states, which was the strange part. The same country, the same minimum wage, the same steamed milk, and completely different floors.

He tested it out loud on Keira, who came in at closing for a hot chocolate she could have made at home for a tenth of the price.

"So my position," he said, wiping her table with unnecessary thoroughness, "is that Rudy's right about Montana, and also that it doesn't matter yet, because I'm still on probation here, and also that 'generally' probably swallows more than Rudy thinks. But I haven't decided how much more. I'm comfortable not deciding."

"That's not a position," Keira said. "That's a shrug with vocabulary."

"It's a considered shrug."

Ms. Demetriou, who had been counting the drawer and, evidently, listening, set down a stack of ones. "Probation's over," she said. "Fourteen days. You show up early, you don't break the cups, you're polite to the man who orders a quad at nine p.m. and then complains about sleeping. You pass."

Dylan felt something in his chest unclench, a small bureaucratic joy, and was halfway through a thank-you when she raised one finger.

"Also, I heard your phone conversation," she said. "I'm from Billings."

He waited.

"We're moving to Missoula in June," she said. "And I'll need someone who can make a latte." She slid a napkin across the counter with an address on it, then picked the napkin back up, wrote something, and slid it over again.

Under the address, in cramped cursive, it said: "Bring the cousin. He sounds insufferable, but he knows his statutes."

"He's not even my employee," Dylan said.

"Neither are you yet," said Ms. Demetriou, and turned off the espresso machine.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Papers posted on arXiv, the preprint server Paul Ginsparg started in 1991, are checked by moderators for relevance but are not peer reviewed before they appear.
story:
The sauce smelled of burnt garlic, which meant her mother had been on the phone with the insurance company again. Annabelle set her laptop on the empty chair beside her and twirled forkfuls of penne while her father read the printed pages of her science fair report, holding them at arm's length because he refused to admit he needed glasses.

"Here," he said, tapping paragraph four. "You wrote that microplastics in drinking water change gut bacteria. That's a strong claim. Where's this from?"

"A study," Annabelle said. "It's cited. APA format and everything."

"The citation says arXiv." He pronounced it like a brand of crackers. "What is that, a journal?"

She felt the floor tilt slightly, the way it did when a teacher called on her and she realized she had been nodding along to something she hadn't actually read. "It's, um. Online. It has physics papers, biology, math. Really current stuff."

"Current how?"

Savannah had sent her the link three weeks ago with the message "this is so us, we're basically plastic people already," and Annabelle had built two pages of argument on it because the abstract had the exact phrasing she needed. She took out her phone under the table and typed "arXiv what is it" with her thumb, shielding the screen from her mother's peripheral vision, which was weapon-grade.

The first result was the site's own About page, and she read it twice, chewing slowly to buy time. It said that arXiv was a preprint server that Paul Ginsparg started in 1991. Papers posted there were checked by moderators for relevance, but they were not peer reviewed before they appeared. She read the last part a third time, then once more, because it refused to rearrange itself into something more convenient. Not peer reviewed. Not checked by experts before the world could read it. The paper she had treated as settled science had never been through the gate she had assumed existed.

"It's a preprint server," she said, and the sentence came out steadier than she felt. "Started by a guy named Paul Ginsparg, in 1991. So it's been around forever. Moderators do check the papers, but only for relevance." She pushed a piece of penne to the rim of her plate. "They're not peer reviewed before they appear."

Her father lowered the pages. "So you cited something nobody verified."

"That's not what I said."

"That is what you just said."

"No. It means it hasn't been verified yet. There's a difference." She was aware that she was defending a position she had discovered ninety seconds ago, and that this was a family trait, and that her mother was now watching them both with the sullen patience of someone who had refereed this exact format for sixteen years.

Annabelle went upstairs after dinner, past her brother's door, where something was being drummed on that was not a drum, and opened her laptop on her bed. She searched for the paper's title plus the word "replication." Nothing. She searched the title plus "follow-up" and found a second study, smaller, different lab, that found no effect at all. The counterpoint was brutal in its plainness: different mice, different doses, no change in gut bacteria. She sat with that for a while, the radiator ticking under the window, the smell of burnt garlic still clinging to her hair.

Then came the twist, which she found at eleven p.m. by following the co-author list like a thread. The second study had cited the first, and a third study, which sounded supportive in its abstract, turned out to share two authors with the first, the same lab, the same mice order form. Three papers, one independent. She laughed once, alone, out of sheer embarrassment at her earlier self, the girl who had written "multiple studies confirm" in a font she had chosen for its authority.

The next morning she knocked on Mr. Ma's door with the report and two granola bars, because he had a poster of Feynman in his hallway and had once let her borrow a book about statistics that she had read half of. He listened while she explained the citation, the preprint server, the replication that wasn't quite a replication, eating one of the granola bars she had brought for herself.

"So what do I do?" she asked. "I can't cite it like it's fact. But I can't pretend it doesn't exist either."

"Which one feels like lying?" Mr. Ma asked.

"Citing it like fact. Obviously."

"And the other option?"

"Hiding it feels like lying too. Just quieter."

He handed back the report and kept the granola bar, which she chose not to interpret as payment for services. At lunch she found Savannah and Christian at the long table by the window and slid into the seat across from them. "My microplastics paper is a disaster," she said, unwrapping a sandwich. "But I think I'm going to present it anyway. As a disaster with structure." Christian, who had cited the same paper in his own report, went very still over his fries. Annabelle tore her sandwich in half and pushed the larger piece across the table. "Check your sources," she said. "And check who wrote them, and who wrote those."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO credit score, making up about 35 percent of it for the general population.
story:
Nicholas had the letter folded into his back pocket for two days before he showed anyone, and by the time he unfolded it at the lunch table the creases had gone soft as cloth. It was from the phone company, and the important part was one line near the bottom: a past due balance of thirty-seven dollars, now forty-one, because a late fee had been added. He had forgotten the first bill ever sent in his own name, and the extra four dollars had arrived like an answer to a question he hadn't known he was asking.

"That's interest," Zara said, tapping the number with one finger. "Well, a fee. But it's the same idea. Borrowed money costs more the longer you take to give it back."

Nicholas looked at the forty-one dollars and then at his tray, where the cafeteria had charged him four seventy-five for a slice of pizza that was mostly crust. "So the longer I wait, the bigger it gets."

"It's not a punishment, exactly. It's the price of using someone else's money." She pulled out her phone, and he watched her thumb move with the certainty of someone who had looked this up before, probably at one in the morning, probably in the dark. "My sister checks her FICO score like it's a weather report. She missed a student loan payment once and talked about it for a month."

Beau slid into the seat across from them, late as always, carrying a chocolate milk he had cajoled out of the cashier by promising to bring exact change tomorrow, a promise they both knew was fictional. He leaned over Zara's shoulder. "What are we panicking about?"

"My credit," Nicholas said, and saying it out loud made it sound both enormous and absurd. He was seventeen. He owned a bike with a bent fender and a sock drawer with eleven dollars in coins.

Beau laughed, but Zara didn't. "It matters," she said. "My sister said payment history is the biggest part of it. Like thirty-five percent. One missed payment and it's the heaviest thing dragging on you." She said it plainly, the way she reported everything, as if the fact had been sitting in her pocket all morning waiting for a reason to come out.

Thirty-seven dollars, then. He did the walk to the phone store after school, past the field where Ms. Augustin was running drills for the JV team, and paid the balance at the counter in cash, counting out ones and quarters while the guy behind the register watched with a patience that cost him something. The receipt said PAID IN FULL. Nicholas folded it next to the letter in his back pocket, two creased pages now, like a small file.

That night he opened a savings account online, because Zara had mentioned hers, and he read the fine print twice, which was one more time than he had ever read the phone contract. The rate was small, a fraction of a percent, and he sat with the strangeness of that for a while: the same force that had grown his debt could, in a different direction, grow his money. He deposited sixty dollars from his bike-repair money and set an automatic transfer for every payday. Then he set the phone bill to autopay, and the phone bill's autopay, and felt briefly, dangerously in control of his life.

Ms. Augustin caught him in the hallway on Thursday. She taught econ and had a way of looking at students as if they were graphs with unlabeled axes. "I heard you've become a person with opinions about compound interest," she said.

"I forgot a bill," he said. "It cost me four dollars."

"And what did the four dollars buy you?"

He thought about it. "Attention, maybe." She nodded once, as if he'd answered correctly, and moved on, and he stood in the hallway feeling like he'd passed a test he hadn't known he was taking.

In study hall he tried to hold both ideas in his head at once, the way he was learning to do in essays: that the same percentage could be a weight or a lift depending on which side of it you stood, and that his own behavior, the boring fact of whether he paid things on time, was apparently the single largest ingredient in a number that would decide things for him before he'd decided anything. What he couldn't figure out was whether the system was fair or just simple, or whether those were different. He wrote "35%" in the margin of his notebook and underlined it, and then felt the pen hesitate, because he didn't actually know yet how much his one mistake had cost him. The number might already be lower. It might not have moved at all. He would not know until he could see it, and he couldn't see it yet, and he had to be honest with himself that this bothered him more than the four dollars had.

Beau, meanwhile, had decided the whole thing was hilarious. He had begun referring to Nicholas as "my financially literate friend" and asking him questions at volume in the locker room, and on Friday he produced, with great ceremony, a pre-approved credit card application he'd gotten in the mail, addressed to him, with a rate on it that made Nicholas's stomach fold in on itself. Beau waved it like a flag. "They want me, Nicky. They see something in me."

"What they see is that you owe the cafeteria four seventy-five," Zara said, not looking up from her book.

Nicholas took the offer out of Beau's hand and read it, all of it, every line of it, while Beau tried to snatch it back, and the rate was high, and the late fee was higher, and it was all right there in print that almost nobody read. "You could get it," he said finally, "and pay it off every month, and it would actually help you. Or you could do what I did and forget one month." He handed it back. "I'm not going to tell you what to do."

"You've changed," Beau said, wounded and delighted at once. "Six months ago you were normal."

Two weeks later, Nicholas's first statement arrived, and he sat on the porch steps to open it, the envelope thin as a leaf. His sixty dollars had earned eleven cents. He stared at the number for a long moment, then laughed out loud alone on the steps, eleven cents, a whole month of patience, and behind the sound of his own laughing he heard the screen door and Beau's voice saying, "So I got the card," and Nicholas turned around, still holding the statement, as Beau held up a brand-new rectangle of silver plastic and grinned.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
Victor had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before closing, three books open in front of him and a photocopied page from Jane Eyre weighted down with his keys. Mr. Nkosi had assigned them a short essay: read the passage where Jane first arrives at Thornfield, then apply either a feminist or a Marxist critical lens, and Victor had spent the week avoiding the assignment because he did not actually know what a lens was supposed to do to a sentence.

He underlined the line where the housekeeper leads Jane through cold corridors to a small room and leaves her there, and beside it he wrote, in the margin, "who owns this house?" That felt Marxist, he thought, or at least economic. Then he wrote, underneath it, "who gets a room?" and was not sure what to do with that.

Nicholas dropped his bag on the opposite chair without asking, because that was how Nicholas entered rooms. He was eating a granola bar he had clearly brought from home, and when he saw the photocopy he leaned over and read it upside down, which he could do, a trick that had won him two dollars off Ilias once. "You're doing the Nkosi thing," he said. "Ilias finished his last night."

"I haven't started."

"You're lying. That's underlining all over it."

"I'm staring at it. That's different." Victor slid the page across anyway. "Okay. Jane shows up at this house with literally nothing, right. No money, no family. The house belongs to a man she's never met. So I want to say something about class, about how she's totally dependent, but then the part that actually stays with me is the room part. She gets this little cold room and it's hers, for now, and the book treats it like it matters. And I can't tell if that's a class thing or a woman thing or if those are even separate here."

Nicholas chewed for a while, which he did when he was actually thinking rather than performing thinking. Then he said, "A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction."

"Is that a quote or a dare."

"It's Woolf. A Room of One's Own, 1929. Ilias made me read a chapter of it Tuesday because he was ranting about the reading list." Nicholas pulled the book out of his bag, because of course he had it, dog-eared and shed-checked from the library shelves an hour ago. "He asked Nkosi in class why so few classic novels on the list were written by women, and Nkosi said 'good question, hold that,' which is his way of not answering, so Ilias answered himself."

Victor took the book. It was thinner than he'd expected, and the prose was quicker, more conversational than the novels on the list. He read a page standing up, one hand on the chair back, and the argument assembled itself in his head almost before he could historicize it: money and a room, five hundred a year of settled income, an annuity rather than a patron's whim, and the whole web of consequence that followed from whether a writer could be shut out of libraries and forced to work in a corridor. "So it's both," he said slowly. "The room is a material thing. Floor, walls, a door that locks. And it's also the condition for the writing. You can't separate the economics from the, I don't know, the permission."

"There you go. Essay's basically done. Want to get food."

"No, wait." Victor sat back down and pulled the photocopy toward him. "But Woolf's talking about writing. Jane Eyre isn't a room of her own in the Woolf sense, it's a room a man lets her have, and he could take it back. That's the Marxist reading, that even her privacy is rented." He was writing fast now, the pen skipping. "But Brontë wrote the book. So Brontë is the one who needed the room, and Jane is the one who dramatizes the need. The character lacks what the author had to fight for. Is that too neat?"

"It's extremely neat. Nkosi will love it or hate it."

"That's the whole problem with him."

Nicholas finished the granola bar, folded the wrapper into a small square, and pocketed it instead of leaving it on the table, a habit his mother had drilled into him and which he performed even here, where someone was paid to clear things away. He watched Victor write for a minute, then said, "You're going to leave out the part you're unsure about, aren't you."

Victor's pen stopped. "Which part."

"Whether the class reading and the feminist reading are one thing or two. You just said you couldn't tell. You'll write around it so it looks like you decided."

The library was emptying around them. Mr. Nkosi was not here tonight, but Victor could picture him at his desk on Monday, reading the stack, able to smell a hedge from three sentences away. He thought about Woolf again, about how she had written the whole book around a question she admitted she couldn't settle, had walked up to the library door and been turned away and simply reported it, without pretending the answer was tidy.

Victor turned to a fresh page and wrote: "What I cannot resolve is whether Jane's dependence and Jane's womanhood are two forces in the novel or one force seen twice." He read it over. It looked naked on the page, like admitting something at a party, but it also looked true, which the neat version had not.

"There," Nicholas said, reading it upside down. "Nkosi's going to write 'good' in the margin and circle it twice. That's his highest honor, I've seen it once, on Ilias's antithesis paper." He stood, shouldered his bag, and waited while Victor packed, then waited again while Victor went back for the Woolf and checked it out at the desk, the cashier of nothing, the librarian stamping the due date while Victor held the book flat against his chest like something borrowed against real odds. "Bring it Tuesday," Nicholas said at the door. "Ilias wants it next."

fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
The dress lay on the bed in two versions of the same problem. The blue one Mina had approved over text, the black one Brooklyn had bought alone on Tuesday and told nobody about, and between them her phone counting down toward seven o'clock, when a boy named after a saint would ring the doorbell and take her to a horror movie she had chosen for reasons she was not ready to examine. She held each dress up to the mirror and watched her face in the glass decide nothing.

Mina arrived first, letting herself in through the back door the way she had since fifth grade, carrying a bag of sour candies and an opinion. "The blue," she said, before hello. "Blue says I'm relaxed. Black says I'm trying." She sat on the floor and started sorting the candies by color, a habit she claimed desensitized her to wanting them all at once, though she ate them anyway, in order.

Briana came twenty minutes later, rain in her hair, apologizing before she was fully through the door. She had walked the long way on purpose, she admitted, because she liked arriving places having already thought about them. "The black," she said, dropping her wet coat on the chair Brooklyn had just cleared. "Black says you know something."

"You don't even know him," Mina said.

"Neither does she. That's the point."

They were talking about the movie now, the one Brooklyn had picked, and Mina was explaining the study she'd found at two in the morning instead of sleeping. "In 1974," she said, "these researchers, Dutton and Aron, had men cross a scary suspension bridge, and there was a woman interviewing them on the other side. The men who crossed the frightening bridge were more likely to call her afterward than men who crossed a sturdy one." She popped a yellow candy. "So. You take him to a horror movie, his heart pounds, and he thinks the pounding is you."

"That's manipulative," Briana said.

"It's chemistry."

"It's lying with someone's body."

Brooklyn stood between them in her bra and jeans, holding the blue dress against her chest, then the black. In the mirror her expression had gone saturnine, the kind of face her mother said she'd inherited from her grandfather, and she caught it and softened it and caught it softening, which was worse. She had spent years watching herself make decisions from a slight distance, a habit her psychology teacher had once labeled metacognition as if naming it made it manageable. It did not make it manageable. It made everything take twice as long.

"Here's what I actually want," she said slowly, and both of them turned, because Brooklyn almost never said what she actually wanted. "I don't want him to leave the theater not knowing what's him and what's the movie. If his heart pounds, I want it to be pounding at me." She laid the blue dress back on the bed. "But I also picked the scary movie because I like scary movies, and if I un-pick it to be honest, then I'm not being me, either."

"Or," Mina said, gentler now, "you tell him. Afterward you say, your heart might be pounding because of the movie or because of me, and there's literally no way for you to know."

"That's a terrible thing to say on a first date," Briana said.

"It's the only true thing."

The doorbell was not the boy; it was Mr. Brennan from next door, holding a package that had been delivered to his porch by mistake, a box of granola bars her mother had ordered. He looked at the three of them, at the dresses on the bed, at the candy sorted into doomed little rows, and asked if something was happening tonight. Brooklyn heard herself tell him about the date, the movie, and Mina's study, all of it tumbling out in the doorway while the rain picked up behind him. He laughed, not unkindly. "When I was your age," he said, "we just hoped for the best." Then he handed her the box and went back out into it.

When the doorbell rang again it was 6:58 and she was in the black dress with the blue one still visible on the bed behind her, a kind of honesty, a kind of lie. Mina and Briana had retreated to the kitchen to eavesdrop with the door cracked. Brooklyn opened the door. The boy stood there with rain on his shoulders and flowers he had clearly been told to buy, holding them the way people hold things they don't know the protocol for.

"There's been a change of plan," she said. "Sort of. We're still seeing the scary movie. But afterward, when your heart's pounding, I need to tell you something about a bridge."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data.
story:
Noemie opened her laptop at her grandmother's kitchen table, between a bowl of walnuts and a jar of pens that smelled of dust. The screen reflected the window, the apple tree, the long grass her grandfather had not yet cut. She had promised herself she would finish the assignment before the weekend ended, and now the weekend was ending around her in the form of her grandmother's Sunday soup, which had to simmer for two hours and could not be hurried any more than the code could.

The task was to write a class in Java with private fields and getter methods, then test it. Her screen held eleven lines so far, and every one of them felt like a sentence in a language she could read but not yet speak. She typed a field, deleted it, typed it again. Behind her, her grandmother moved between the stove and the sink, impervious to the small crisis unfolding at the table, humming something from a radio program that had been cancelled decades ago.

Noemie kept thinking about Tuesday, at coding club, when she had lambasted Anis in front of everyone for reorganizing the shared project files without asking. She had gone on for a full minute, and Melina had watched her with a flatness that was worse than argument. Then Anis had opened the project and shown her what he had done: he had changed a field's type in one of the classes, and nothing else had broken. Not one other file. Noemie had stopped mid-sentence, and the silence had been its own kind of information.

She had not understood, at first, why it worked. She had gone home and opened the class and looked. The fields were private. Other code reached them only through methods, through getters, and as long as the getters kept their names and returned sensible values, the rest of the program went on believing nothing had changed. The class had become like her grandmother's soup: everyone at the table received a bowl, and nobody needed to know what went on inside the pot.

"Your mother says you are doing the computer science," her grandmother said, not turning from the stove.

"It's a program. You build a... a kind of container, and you keep things inside it, and other parts of the program ask it for things instead of reaching in." Noemie was testing the idea out loud, the way you test a stone before stepping on it.

Her grandmother tapped the pot lid with her wooden spoon. "So the soup is not on the table, only in bowls."

"Sort of," Noemie said, though she suspected the analogy was generous, and said so.

On the screen she wrote the field as private, then wrote a getter, then a small test class with a main method that made an object and printed what came back. She ran it. Nothing printed, because she had misspelled the method name, and the compiler told her so in language that felt personal for about four seconds before she remembered it was not. She fixed it and ran it again, and this time the value appeared, correct and small and green.

She thought again about Tuesday, about her minute of speech in front of the whole club. She had defended her position on the file reorganization as a matter of principle, of respect for shared work, and part of her still held that. But another part, the part now typing assertions into a test file, kept noticing that Anis's change had been safe precisely because the code was built to allow change, and that she had not even looked before she had spoken. Two ways of thinking about the same afternoon sat in her without merging. She could not yet say which one she would follow the next time, and she was tired of pretending that not deciding was the same as not caring.

Melina had texted her that night with a single line: "He did ask me first, just so you know." Noemie had typed three replies and sent none of them, and the unsent drafts were still sitting in her head, a substrate for feelings she had not sorted. She picked up her phone now, looked at the thread, and put it down again.

Instead she opened a new class in the editor. She built it the way the good ones were built: private fields, methods standing at the door, asking what was wanted. Then, on an impulse she did not fully examine, she changed one field's type and ran the tests again. All of them passed. It felt a little like a trick and a little like a promise, and she could not have said which, and she noticed that she did not mind.

"Encapsulation," she said quietly, mostly to the soup.

"What is that word?" her grandmother asked.

"It means hiding a class's data behind methods," Noemie said, "so other code can use it without knowing how it stores things." Her grandmother nodded slowly, as though this confirmed something she had suspected about pots for years.

Noemie saved the file, then picked up the phone and typed to Melina: "Ask Anis if the club can look at my test class tomorrow. I want to show them something." She pressed send before she could unwrite it, and outside, under the apple tree, the long grass bent all at once in the wind.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: If a Java class defines no constructor, the compiler adds a default no-argument one; once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added.
story:
The coding club met in the back corner of the library on Thursdays, where the radiators clanked and Mr. Xu kept a tin of shortbread he pretended not to share. Jesse arrived late, laptop under his arm, because he had spent the bus ride reading the chapter twice and still did not trust it. His problem was simple to say and hard to hold: the portfolio he wanted to submit with his college application needed something better than the tip calculator he had written in October, and Mr. Xu had told him that if he was serious, he should learn to build a class the way adults built them, with private fields and getter methods, and then test it.

"Private fields," Diya said, when he sat down across from her. "So nobody can just reach in and change them."

"That's the idea." He opened his laptop and started typing. He made a class called Student, gave it private fields for name and grade, and wrote methods that handed the values back out, one at a time. It felt strange, almost ceremonial, like wrapping things in paper before giving them away. In his test file he wrote a line that created a Student and set its fields, and the little green bar at the bottom of the screen told him everything passed.

Mr. Xu drifted past, looked over his shoulder, and said nothing, which Jesse had learned to read as approval.
