Diya, meanwhile, was arguing with Constance about whether a class should ever let its fields be changed after creation. Constance, nonchalant, spinning a pen between her fingers, said that mutable state was fine as long as you were the only one touching it. "That's how you become a despot," Diya said. "Ruling over your own data with no accountability." Jesse smiled at that, but privately he thought Constance had a point. He was the only one touching this code. Privacy seemed like a lot of ceremony for a program with one author.

So he pushed further. He added a constructor that took the name and grade as parameters, so a Student could be born already filled in, instead of being created empty and then assigned piece by piece. It was cleaner, he thought, the way a sentence with the subject attached is cleaner than a sentence waiting for one. He wrote it, compiled it, ran his test.

The green bar turned red.

He stared at the failure for a long moment, then leaned toward Diya's screen as if her code might explain his. The message pointed at the line in his old test, the one where he created a Student and then set the fields. He checked the constructor first, letter by letter. Then he checked the test, though he had not touched it. Diya watched him cycle between the two files three times before she said, "Wait. What did you change?"

"Only the constructor." As he said it, something shifted in his head, the way a picture flips when you have stared at it too long. Before he had written any constructor, the test had worked anyway, which meant something had been there when he wasn't looking. He scrolled up, deleted his constructor entirely, and ran the test again. Green. He re-added it, exactly as before. Red. He sat back and let out a breath. "It was there before," he said slowly. "And then I wrote mine, and it wasn't."

Constance had rolled her chair over by then, chin on her folded arms. "It was there before what?"

"Before I wrote any constructor," Jesse said. "If a class defines no constructor, the compiler adds a default one, a no-argument one. But once you write any constructor of your own, that default isn't added anymore." He heard the sentence come out of him and realized it was the first thing in the chapter he actually believed, because he had broken it and watched it break. His old test had been calling a constructor that had stopped existing the moment he gave the class a better one.

He fixed the test to use his new constructor, and the bar went green, and for a second he felt the clean, absolute pleasure of it. Then a small deflation followed, which he did not mention to anyone. The old test, the first one, the one that had worked all on its own, was gone now; he had overwritten it, and its passing had been invisible to him while it lasted. He saved a copy of the broken version in a folder called notes so he could look at it later. Mr. Xu came by with the shortbread tin and set two pieces on the table between Jesse and Diya, which was his way of allaying, or trying to allay, the general anxiety of portfolio season without saying a word about it.

Jesse wrote the fixed test, then a second one, then a third, checking each field as it came back out through the getter methods. Around him the club argued on, Constance insisting that rules were only rules when someone else had to follow them, Diya writing unit tests for her own class like a small tribunal. Jesse half-agreed with both of them and committed to neither. He looked at his class, with its private fields, its one constructor, its careful doors, and understood that he had traded something for the order, though he could not yet have said what. He ran the suite once more anyway. Green bar, six tests, radiator clanking under the window.

"Show me the trick," Constance said, pulling her chair around. "The one where it breaks."

Jesse deleted his constructor, watched her watch the test pass, then typed it back in.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius.
story:
The graph came out of the printer crooked, one corner curling, and Chase smoothed it flat on the lab bench before Ms. Mercer could see that his hand had been less steady than he'd pretended. Keeling curve, she'd called it, though she hadn't told them what to say about it. That was the assignment: each of them had to stand up on Friday and explain, in plain words, how greenhouse gases trap heat, using the graph as evidence. She'd written one question on the board and left it there all week. Is the greenhouse effect a problem, or is it something we can't live without? Chase had copied it into his notebook and then sat looking at it, because he didn't actually know yet, and he hated not knowing.

He'd been to the planetarium with Iain and Priscilla in eighth grade, the year before everything between the three of them got complicated. They'd sat in the dark under a projected Moon, gray and pocked, and Iain had leaned over and whispered that the Moon was the same distance from the sun as Earth, so why was it a frozen rock at night while Earth wasn't. Priscilla, who read astronomy books for fun, had said it was because Earth had something the Moon didn't, gases in the air that held on to heat, and without them Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14. Iain had argued with her anyway, because that was what Iain did. So the gases are bad, he'd said, everyone says they're bad. They can't be both. Priscilla had shrugged in the dark. Why not?

Chase thought about that argument now more than he'd expected to. He and Iain hadn't spoken since spring, since the thing at Iain's house that Chase still couldn't sort into a single clean feeling: a fight about nothing, or a fight about everything, the usual morass of a friendship ending in slow motion. The incipient silence between them had been growing for months before that night, and Chase had let it grow, telling himself it would pass, and it hadn't passed.

In the empty lab after school, he laid the graph out and made himself read it the way Ms. Mercer had taught them, axis by axis. Carbon dioxide, parts per million, year by year across the century. The line climbed in small sawtooth steps, dipping and rising, and then in the last decades it steepened, as if it had decided something. He put his finger at 1960 and slid it up to the present and felt a strange satisfaction, the kind he got from any pattern resolving, and then a stranger unease underneath it, because a pattern wasn't the same as a meaning.

Priscilla came in with her bag over one shoulder and sat down across from him without asking. She could still do that. "You're going first on Friday," she said. "Mercer told me. She said you seemed ready."

"I'm not ready. That's the problem." He turned the graph toward her. "Look, I can explain the mechanism fine. Certain gases let sunlight through and then absorb the heat radiating back off the surface, so the air holds warmth it would otherwise lose. I understand that part. And the graph, I can read the graph. What I can't do is what she's actually asking, which is take a side."

Priscilla pulled the paper closer, and for a moment he was back at the planetarium, her face lit faintly blue, Iain's whispered voice between them. "You remember that day," she said, not quite a question.

"Iain wanted the gases to be the villain. And they're not, exactly. Without the natural greenhouse effect, the planet would be frozen, minus 18, and nothing we recognize survives that. Fourteen degrees, minus 18 degrees, and the second one is a dead world. So the effect itself is the reason we exist. It's like the villain is not the effect but the extras. Too much of something that was keeping us alive." His heart palpitated as he said it, which embarrassed him, because it was only a classroom. "Except I'm not sure I can prove that from a graph. The graph shows a rise. It doesn't show what the rise does, not by itself. I'd be joining two things and acting like they're one."

"So join them and say you're doing it." Priscilla tapped the steep end of the curve. "That's not lying. That's being honest about the seam."

He looked at her, then at the door, half expecting Iain to walk through it the way he used to, late, with some excuse and an opinion nobody had asked for. The door stayed shut. He thought of their last real conversation, how he'd chosen the easy deflection instead of saying what he meant, and how he still didn't know whether the deflection or the silence afterward had been the actual mistake.

On Friday he stood at the front with the crooked graph pinned to the board. "Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly fourteen," he said. "So I'm not going to tell you greenhouse gases are simply bad. I'm going to tell you what the graph shows, what we know about the effect itself, and exactly where my certainty runs out." He uncapped the marker and drew a thin vertical line across the rising curve. "This is the seam. Everything left of it, I can defend. Everything right of it, we're still finding out." Then he stepped back, and Ms. Mercer said, "Go on."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The electron transport chain sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with protons to form water.
story:
Isabelle spread her notes across the hood of the farm truck, weighting the corners with horse-shoe-shaped magnets she'd lifted from the workshop fridge, because the wind on this hilltop treated paper the way the fox treated the henhouse. The biology exam was Monday. It was Saturday. In between stood forty-two heifers, a lamb with scours, and her father's conviction that chores came before chromosomes.

"You're going to fail," said Deegan, who was supposed to be helping her study and was instead throwing pebbles at the water trough. "You still can't get past glycolysis."

"I can get past glycolysis. Glycolysis is fine. Glucose gets split, you get a little ATP, and then everything goes into the krebs cycle like nothing happened." She tapped the diagram with her pencil so hard the tip snapped. "It's after that. The electron transport chain. It's a morass. There are all these carriers and protons and the whole thing just becomes arrows."

"Arrows are the official language of biology," Deegan said solemnly. "My sister eulogized her goldfish with a diagram once. Goldfish to fish tank, fish tank to toilet. Very moving."

Isabelle laughed despite herself, which cost her a gust of wind that stole the page on fermentation and carried it into the paddock, where a heifer named Duchess regarded it with the saturnine indifference of an animal who has seen many papers die. Isabelle climbed the fence, retrieved the page from beneath Duchess's hoof, and stood there a moment in the muddy field, breathing hard.

That was when Ms. Hoang called from the garden fence. She lived on the next property over and kept bees in white boxes that looked like filing cabinets for very small clerks. "Exam?" she asked, nodding at the papers.

"Monday," Isabelle said. "I understand everything except the part where it actually works. Where the ATP comes from. My teacher says the chain is in the inner membrane of the mitochondria, and that's supposed to mean something, and it just doesn't."

Ms. Hoang did not offer wisdom. She offered rhubarb, and the information that she was going to check the hives, and that Isabelle was welcome to come along if she could stop staring at her notes long enough to breathe. Isabelle climbed down off the fence and followed, mostly to get away from Deegan's pebbles.

The bees were working the combers of clover along the fence line, and Ms. Hoang lifted a frame covered in them without hurry. "They fly out," she said, "they find nectar, they bring it back, and it becomes something else entirely. Honey. Different thing altogether." She held the frame so Isabelle could see the cells, some capped with wax, some open and shining. Isabelle looked at the bees, and then, the way a word you've been hunting all day suddenly arrives from nowhere, the diagram reorganized itself in her head. The chain in the inner membrane. Electrons being handed along, carrier to carrier, like the nectar passed from bee to bee. And at the end of it, the last carrier, waiting.

"Oxygen," she said out loud. "Oxygen's the final electron acceptor."

Ms. Hoang only said, "Mm," in the way of a person who does not know what that means but recognizes the sound of something clicking.

"Because the chain sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and oxygen is the final electron acceptor, and it combines with protons and forms water." Isabelle heard her own voice go strange on the last word. "Water. Like, the oxygen I'm breathing right now." She took a breath, deliberately, and let it out. Somewhere inside her, in a number of cells she could not name, that oxygen was going to end up as water. Every breath was a delivery. She thought of the trough, of Duchess drinking, of the rain on the hill, and felt briefly as though she were standing inside an enormous, quiet factory that had been running since before she was born.

She walked back fast, holding the rhubarb, and found Deegan now attempting to teach the lamb to follow him by calling it Steve. "The oxygen becomes water," she announced. "Inside you. Inside your cells. That's what breathing is for."

"That's disturbing," Deegan said. "I preferred it when breathing was just breathing."

She sat on the truck's tailgate and recited the whole pathway for him, glucose to pyruvate to the krebs cycle to the chain in the inner membrane, and when she fumbled the carriers she fumbled them out loud and corrected herself, and Deegan marked her on the diagram with a stub of pink crayon he'd found in the cab, which was the only writing implement on the entire farm. The light went long and gold over the hill. On Monday she would walk into the exam room and take a breath, and somewhere in her, quietly, without her permission, it would become water.

"Duchess ate your fermentation page," Deegan said. "Just so you know."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'.
story:
The spare room at Grandmother's house smelled of lavender and old paper, and it was there, on the third morning of spring break, that Naomi opened her laptop and confronted the problem Angeline had texted her. Their computer science class had split into pairs for a data project, and Angeline, insouciant as ever, had already gone to the beach, leaving Naomi to figure out the hardest query: find which customers had ordered nothing. Two tables sat in the practice database, one of customers, one of orders, and Naomi stared at them the way she used to stare at the pond behind the school, wondering what was underneath the surface.

She typed a first attempt, joining the tables on customer ID. The results came back wrong immediately, because a join like that could only return customers who appeared in both tables, and a customer with no orders appeared nowhere in the orders table at all. It was like searching a room for someone who had never entered it. She deleted the query, sat back, and let the wrongness of it sit there. How did you ask a question about absence? The whole idea felt like trying to photograph silence.

From the kitchen came the small percussion of Grandmother's routine, kettle and spoon and the radio turned low. Last summer Naomi had spent a whole week here teaching Grandmother to use the tablet her son had bought her, and Grandmother had taught Naomi to make the lemon cake in return, refusing to measure anything. "You watch until your hands know," she had said, tipping flour into the bowl with a confidence that made measuring cups seem like a veneer over real knowledge. The flashback surfaced now as Naomi rubbed her eyes: her grandmother's hands, certain and unhurried, the cake turning out perfect anyway.

She tried a different approach. Instead of an inner join, she reached for a left join, keeping every customer from the left table whether or not the right table matched. She ran it. Hundreds of rows came back, every customer listed, and the ones with no orders showed empty cells where order numbers should have been. There they were, visible at last, holes in the data shaped exactly like people. Then she added a WHERE clause on the empty order column and ran it again, and the results narrowed to eleven customers, eleven names attached to nothing.

The doorbell rang, and it was Mr. Menon from next door, come to fix the porch light he had promised Grandmother he would fix, though he lingered first over the cake on the counter. Naomi had known him since she was small, and when he asked what she was doing in the spare room all morning, she showed him the screen, the two tables, the query. She was still puzzling over something, she admitted. Why tables at all? Databases could have been organized any way people wanted, lists or folders or webs, and yet the whole world had settled on rows and columns. Somebody had to have chosen that, and she wanted to know who and why it won.

Mr. Menon smiled and said only that she was asking a better question than most of his colleagues ever had, but he wouldn't spoil it for her, and he went back out to the porch with his screwdriver. It was Grandmother who ended up being the accidental librarian. While Naomi helped clear the table, Grandmother mentioned the box of books her late husband's brother had left, boxes of computer things from his IBM days, up in the hall closet if Naomi wanted something to read that wasn't a screen. So Naomi climbed the stairs, knelt in the hallway, and pulled out a stack of old technical papers and journals, yellow-edged and smelling faintly of the attic.

Halfway through the stack she found it, and the finding enervated her less than it focused her, all her scattered curiosity pouring suddenly into one channel. A paper from 1970, "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks," by an IBM researcher named Edgar F. Codd. The relational model, the idea underlying the tables she had been joining all morning, had been introduced right there. She read the title twice, then sat down on the hallway floor with the paper open across her knees, careful with the brittle pages, and thought about a man at IBM in 1970 deciding that data should live in tables, in relations, so that questions like hers, questions about what was missing, could be asked at all.

She took a photograph of the title page and texted it to Angeline, who replied from the beach with a string of exclamation points and the confession that she had assumed databases had always been tables, the way people assume rivers have always run downhill. Naomi carried the paper downstairs and set it beside her laptop, and ran her query one more time, watching the eleven empty-handed customers appear on the screen. There was still something she couldn't decide, and she turned it over while the kettle ticked in the kitchen: was the query finding the customers who ordered nothing, or was it inventing a category, absence itself, that only existed because the tables made absence visible? The data couldn't tell her whether those eleven people were unhappy, or forgetful, or simply waiting.

The afternoon light moved across the spare room floor. Downstairs, Mr. Menon called out that the porch light was fixed, and Grandmother answered that he would stay for tea and cake, and Naomi heard the cabinet open for the good cups. She closed the laptop halfway, folded her hands on it, and looked at the old paper beside her, its 1970 typeface small and certain.

"Grandmother," she called down the stairwell. "Can Mr. Menon have the piece with the extra lemon? And can we keep the boxes in the closet where they are, just for now?"

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
The gym smelled of rubber mats and the grape electrolyte mix nobody liked, and Ava was holding a clipboard she had not written on once. Her job, Mr. Cheung had said, was to watch Antonin's serves and give him notes by the end of practice. This was a reprieve from running suicide drills, which was the only reason she'd agreed, and it had seemed simple until Antonin's fifth serve went long, his sixth into the net, and Charlie-Rose, folding towels by the bench, said nothing at all.

"He's getting better," Charlie-Rose said when Ava looked at her.

"He's getting worse," Ava said. "You saw the last six."

"I saw a person having a rough day."

Ava wrote nothing. She knew what Charlie-Rose meant, because last season Charlie-Rose had watched Ava shank her tosses for three straight weeks and had said only it's fine, you're fine, and it had beguiled Ava completely, that softness, right up until the regional semifinal when Ava's toss cost them the match. Afterwards Charlie-Rose cried harder than Ava did, which was somehow worse. Being kind had not protected anyone.

Antonin served again, an ugly, turgid thing that floated up like a balloon and died a metre short of the line. Mr. Cheung blew his whistle twice, the signal for water, and wandered off toward the storage room. Ava found him there, ostensibly helping him carry a bag of balls, actually stalling.

"Do I have to say the true thing?" she asked. "The notes thing."

"You have to give notes," Mr. Cheung said, which was not an answer, and he clearly knew it.

She carried the balls back out. Charlie-Rose was sitting on the bench now, scrolling her phone, and she turned the screen when Ava sat down. It was Charlie-Rose's mother's book club page, some management book with a cover like a motivational poster. "My mom won't shut up about this," Charlie-Rose said. "Radical Candor, by Kim Scott, 2017. She says good feedback means you care personally about someone and you challenge them directly. Both. Not one or the other."

"That's the book?" Ava said. "That's the whole thing?"

"My mom says there's a chart."

Antonin came back from the fountain with water down his chin, and practice had twenty minutes left, and Ava understood that whatever she was going to say, she had to say it before Mr. Cheung assembled the circle and asked for her notes out loud, in front of everyone. That was the trap. She could be vague for the team's benefit, or she could be honest in front of eleven people, which felt less like feedback and more like a public stoning.

"Hey," she said to Antonin, quietly enough that only he and Charlie-Rose could hear. "Can I tell you the pattern before Coach makes me say notes to everybody?"

He wiped his chin. "Please."

"Your toss is drifting left. Every serve, about a hand's width. That's why they're going long and short, you're compensating for a toss that isn't where you think it is. It's not your arm. Your arm's fine."

Antonin looked at his left hand like it had betrayed him personally. "You could see that?"

"I watched every serve. I had a clipboard. It looked very official."

He laughed, then got a ball and walked to the line, and Ava felt something settle that she couldn't have named, some small proof that specificity was its own kind of care. She was still not sure it would work. He could toss left forever, for all she knew; one note wasn't a fix, and Charlie-Rose's mom's chart might be nonsense. But Antonin tossed, waited, adjusted, tossed again, and served, and the ball clipped the back line with a sound like a door closing softly.

"THERE," Antonin said, to the ceiling.

"Again," Ava said, and wrote on her clipboard, finally, one line: toss left, hand's width, fixed. Then she crossed out "fixed" and wrote, "mostly."

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Article I, Section 7 of the US Constitution requires all bills for raising revenue to originate in the House of Representatives, though the Senate may amend them.
story:
Sophia had told Angeline, twice, that she had read the whole rulebook, and the second time she almost believed it herself. The model parliament was being held in the district courthouse that Saturday, ninety students in suits and borrowed blazers, and Sophia had been assigned to the Senate, which she had assumed until Thursday night was where the important things happened. That was the trouble with the way she studied: she read until she felt confident, and then she stopped, and the feeling of knowing transmuted itself, quietly, into the thing itself. So she had not read the section on revenue.

Her bill was her own idea, and she was proud of it in a way that made her careful. It proposed a small levy on plastic packaging, with the money earmarked for river cleanup, and she had drafted it at her kitchen table with her mother leaning over her shoulder suggesting commas. In committee that morning, Maximilien had picked it apart with something like affection. "You can't just say the money goes to rivers," he said, tapping her clause three. "You have to appropriate it. Otherwise the treasury is just holding it." Around the long table the other committee members marked up her paper, and Angeline slid her a note that read, "He's helping, I promise," which Sophia chose not to fully believe, because Maximilien had run against her for the Senate seat and had lost by four votes and had been noncommittal about it ever since.

The committee reported the bill out with amendments, and the schedule said Senate debate at two o'clock. Sophia stood in the corridor eating a granola bar, rehearsing her opening, when Mr. Sinclair, the teacher running the parliament, passed by with a stack of folders. He paused. "Which chamber are you in?" he asked, and when she said the Senate, he looked at her bill folder, and then at her, and said only, "Read your rulebook, section on revenue, before you go in." He did not explain, which annoyed her, and then frightened her a little, because Mr. Sinclair never told anyone to read anything unless it mattered.

She sat on the courthouse steps with the rulebook open on her knees. There it was, in plain print: all bills for raising revenue must originate in the House of Representatives. The Senate could amend such bills, but it could not start them. Her levy was revenue. Her bill had originated in the Senate, in her own kitchen, in her own name. She read the clause three times, as if reading it slowly might make it say something else. Angeline came out and sat down beside her, and Sophia said, without looking up, "I've been telling people I read this whole thing." Angeline didn't say anything comforting, which was the right choice, and instead took the rulebook and read the clause herself.

They had twenty minutes. Angeline was in the House; that was the luck of it. "I'll introduce it there," she said. "You write the amendments from the committee. We can still make the debate slot if the House moves it after lunch." Sophia sat on the steps drafting on the back of her folder, copying out the amended clauses in her fastest handwriting, and when she handed the pages over she said, "The sponsorship has to be yours. Your name on it. I can't have my name on it." Angeline looked at her for a second too long, and Sophia understood that this was a real gift she was asking for, the credit for a bill Sophia had written, and that Angeline was giving it anyway.

While the House debated it, Sophia stood at the back of that chamber, where she was technically out of order, and watched Maximilien argue against the levy on the grounds that it punished small businesses, which was a fair point she had not put in her own opening speech. She found herself writing his argument down so she could answer it, which felt like a strange kind of respect. When the division bell rang, the House passed it, 41 to 38, and the bill went across the hall to the Senate as an amendment, and Sophia stood at her desk and argued for her own bill as amended by her friend under her friend's name, answering Maximilien point by point, conceding the small-business clause to him with a nod that he returned.

At the end of the afternoon the Speaker of the model parliament signed the bill in a ceremony that took four minutes, a pen scratching on paper under the courtroom's tall windows, and Mr. Sinclair called it assent and said something brief about how a law was now made. Everyone applauded. Sophia applauded too, and then stopped, because she was trying to work out what exactly she had accomplished: a bill that was hers in every way except the one that the record would show. She was still turning it over when Maximilien sat down beside her in the emptied chamber.

"You know I voted for it," he said. "After you conceded the exemption. That was the right way to lose an argument." He pulled a folded page from his jacket, the committee markup of her original draft, with his own handwriting in the margins. "You should keep this. The Senate version. It's not the one that passed, but it's the one that started everything." Sophia took the page and read the first line, where he had written his amendment in small, careful letters: the packaging levy, with restitution to affected businesses, struck through and rewritten softer.

Later, on the bus home, she texted Angeline: "I told everyone I read the rulebook. I hadn't. The bill exists because you did the part I couldn't." The reply came after a long pause, long enough that Sophia watched the river go by outside the window and decided Angeline was annoyed, or generous, or thinking, or all three. Then the phone buzzed. "Next year you read the whole thing and I sponsor nothing," Angeline wrote, followed by a single line Sophia read four times: "It's our bill. I don't want it back."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US Fair Labor Standards Act took effect on October 24, 1938, setting the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour and a maximum workweek of 44 hours.
story:
The schedule went up on the break room door on a Tuesday, and Clara counted her hours twice before she let herself react. Nineteen hours at the bakery, spread across six closing shifts, at the state minimum, which after taxes left her short of the deposit for the dorm. She photographed the schedule with her phone and said nothing to the manager, because her mother had said nothing to managers for twenty years and Clara had watched where that went.

On Wednesday, Ms. Morales put a question on the board before the bell finished ringing: what did the government owe a worker, and what did a worker owe the employer who signed the checks? Arnaud, who argued the way other people breathed, was talking before anyone else could. "The employer took the risk," he said. "He bought the ovens. He can set the price of the labour." Nour, two seats over, turned around in her chair. "He also set your hours, Arnaud. Six closings a week isn't a schedule, it's a siege."

Clara kept her hand down. She had wanted to say that her manager called the shifts voluntary, which was a word that meant nothing when the answer to "can you close tomorrow" was always yes or fewer hours forever. But she was aware of knowing it only from the inside, from the smell of proofing dough at eleven at night, and she distrusted arguments she could feel in her stomach. She wanted numbers. She wanted the kind of fact Arnaud couldn't call sentiment.

Ms. Morales had left a carton of primary sources on the side table, yellowed reproductions she called her archaeology kit. Clara stayed after the bell while Nour waited by the window, and dug past union charters and photographs of picket lines. She found a one-page excerpt from a federal statute, and read it standing up, one finger on the date. The Fair Labor Standards Act, it said, had taken effect on October 24, 1938, and had set the first federal minimum wage at twenty-five cents an hour, with a maximum workweek of forty-four hours. Twenty-five cents. Forty-four hours. She copied both onto her wrist in pen, the way she copied oven temperatures, then wrote the date twice so she couldn't transpose it.

"Find something?" Nour said.

"October 24, 1938," Clara said. "That's when it started. First federal minimum wage in the country, twenty-five cents an hour. And they capped the workweek at forty-four hours, right in the law."

"So the siege has a legal ceiling," Nour said.

"Ceilings move," Clara said. "That one took a whole law to build."

That night she sat cross-legged on her bed with the schedule photo and her phone's calculator, not exactly thinking but not resting either, doing the arithmetic her father would have called cogitating with a purpose. Twenty-five cents in 1938, forty-four hours as a national limit. Her grandfather had been a labourer then, an autodidact who taught himself contract language from library books and read the fine print aloud at kitchen tables where men signed things they couldn't parse. She'd heard the story all her life without ever asking what the numbers underneath it were. Both of them, her mother's silence and her grandfather's reading aloud, were answers to the same question, and she had been choosing between them without noticing she was choosing.

Friday, Arnaud brought his bellicose best. "Minimum wages kill jobs," he said, slapping the table. "You force a price on labour and the employer buys less of it. It's arithmetic."

"Then explain 1938 to me," Clara said, and she said it flat, no performance. "October 24, the Fair Labor Standards Act takes effect. Twenty-five cents an hour, forty-four hours max, first time the whole country had a floor. The floor was the argument. People decided a workweek could be too long and a wage too low, and they didn't ask permission from the arithmetic."

"Twenty-five cents was worth more then," Arnaud said.

"It was worth the fight," Clara said. "That's the part I can prove."

But at the bakery on Saturday, closing alone because the other part-timer had quit over the new schedule, Clara mopped the floor and was honest with herself in the small tiled quiet. She didn't know whether the union sticker she'd put in her locker would survive her needing the job through spring. She didn't know if Nour would still want to hand out the pay sheet they'd made, with everyone's hours on it, when the manager found out. The law had drawn a line once, in 1938, and people had stepped over it and been made to step back, and other people had held the line for years she would never see. She only knew which side of the door she was standing on.

At 11:40 she clocked out and found the other part-timer waiting by the racks, the one who was supposed to have quit, back for a forgotten jacket and lingering.

"They cut my Tuesday," he said. "And I heard the new girl gets less than we do."

Clara pulled the pay sheet from her apron pocket and held it out flat on the steel counter. "Write your number down," she said. "We're doing the math together this time."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
Annabelle carried the crate of tomatoes across the market lot with both arms, the wood flexing under the weight, and set it down beside the folding table where her mother was arranging jars of chutney. The market had thinned to its last hour, the awnings snapping in a wind that had come up around noon, and the July heat still pressed down on the gravel like a hand. In the crate beside the tomatoes sat two blocks of cheese, a coil of sausage, and a pint of cream, all of it bought at eleven that morning and all of it meant for the dinner she had promised to cook.

She had planned the meal for two weeks: a tomato sauce with the sausage browned in butter, the cream folded in at the end, everything served over the pasta her father liked. It was a small thing to want, to be the one who made it, but her mother worked Saturdays at the market stall and her father worked the late shift, and the cooking had a way of falling to whoever was home first, which lately was nobody. Tonight, her mother had acceded to the plan with a shrug that Annabelle chose to read as permission rather than indifference.

"Your friend's over by the honey," her mother said, nodding toward the row of white canopies. Izabella was walking between the stalls with her hands in her pockets, reticent as always in crowds, watching the ground until she was close enough to speak. She and Annabelle had been assigned a summer project on food policy, and she had come to the market partly for research and partly, Annabelle suspected, because there was nothing else to do.

They helped load the van. The cheese and sausage went into a cooler with the cream, and Annabelle noticed that the ice packs had gone soft, more water than ice, sloshing under the lids. She held one up and let it drip onto the gravel. "We've been here since eight," her mother said, taking it from her. "It held."

They could not leave, though. Mr. Leblanc, who kept the stall two spots down, needed help breaking down his tables, and he paid in vegetables, and his beans were better than anything at the grocery store. Annabelle and Izabella carried crates of squash and stacked the folding legs while the sun moved a slow degree westward. Mr. Leblanc talked the whole time about his grandfather's orchard, and about a colloquialism from his childhood, "keeping the flies off it," which meant keeping food from spoiling, though he had never once wondered, he admitted, how it actually worked.

That was the sentence Annabelle kept returning to as she stacked the last crate. On the drive home she took out her phone and searched for how long food could sit out, mostly to settle a feeling she could not name. What she found stopped her: perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees. She read it twice. The cooler had been closed but the van had been parked in full sun, and the market had been running since morning, and it was well past ninety out.

"Annabelle, it's fine," her mother said when she raised it, but she said it without force, the way she said things when she had not thought about them yet. Annabelle sat with the cheese and the sausage on the counter and did the arithmetic out loud. Bought at eleven. Loaded into the van at two. Mr. Leblanc's tables until almost three, then the drive home. Four hours, maybe more, and the ice packs soft, and everything inside warmer than the refrigerator and cooler than the stove, which was the range she was not supposed to trust.

Izabella, still in the kitchen filling out the project notes, looked up from her laptop. "So what do you do?" she asked. It was the practical question, and it was also, Annabelle realized, the question their whole project kept circling. You could throw everything out and waste a family's groceries, or you could serve them and risk making everyone sick, and no one could tell you which was right without telling you how much risk, and no one would tell her that. She could be careful or she could be generous with the food, and she could not fully be both.

She cooked the sauce with the tomatoes, which had sat out all day but were whole and uncut, and she was careful with those too, washing each one under the tap. The cheese and the sausage she wrapped and put in the trash, and the cream went with them, and when her mother came into the kitchen and saw, she stood in the doorway for a moment and then reached past Annabelle for the pot lid without a word.

They ate at seven, her father home early for once, twirling the pasta and asking twice what was in the sauce that made it so bright. Annabelle told him about the market, and about Mr. Leblanc's beans, and about the four hours the cooler had sat in the sun, though she left out the part where she had almost served it anyway. Izabella stayed for dinner and took the last of the bread. Afterward, drying the pot while her mother washed it, Annabelle looked at the two of them in the window's reflection, the kitchen lit yellow behind them, the yard gone dark. "Next week I'm bringing real ice," she said, and her mother laughed and handed her the pot.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: A force majeure clause frees the parties from their obligations when an extraordinary event outside their control, such as a natural disaster or war, prevents them from performing.
story:
The rental counter at the airport had a line of eleven people and one agent, and Seth's mother had put him in charge of the paperwork because she claimed her hands were full, though her hands were holding nothing but her phone. Behind them, an ebullient man in a golf shirt was telling anyone who would listen that the storm had been "the best thing that ever happened to the conference," since attendance was mandatory now that nobody could fly out. Seth was not sure he agreed, but the man had a point in there somewhere, folded in with everything else.

The problem was simple. His mother had reserved a midsize sedan for the drive to Merlefest, where Tessa and Arthur were already camped out with the tickets Seth had paid for, forty dollars each, from two months of bagging groceries. The storm had closed the airport and half the highway. The rental company, per the agent, a patient man named Mr. Lim, now had no midsize sedans and possibly no cars at all, and the question on the counter between them was whether the reservation was a promise or only a suggestion.

"Your mother signed the rental agreement," Mr. Lim said, turning the screen toward her, then, since she was still on her phone, toward Seth. "The terms and conditions apply."

Seth read them. He read them the way he read everything, fast first, then slower, because the fast pass had caught a phrase that seemed to belong to a different language, one where ordinary events wore formal clothing. There was a whole section about liability, which the agreement placed almost entirely on the renter, and a shorter section, near the end, in a smaller font, headed "Force Majeure."

"You keep saying your hands are full," he said to his mother. "You could hold the tablet."

"You're doing great," she said, which was what she always said when she had decided something was his job.

He read the clause through twice. It said the company was released from its obligations when extraordinary events outside its control, natural disasters among them, prevented performance. Performance, in this language, did not mean a concert. It meant doing what you had promised, and the clause meant that the storm had let the company off the hook before Seth's mother had even reached the counter. He checked the reverse direction and found it quieter but present: the clause protected both parties, not just the big one. If a hurricane stranded the car in another state, his mother would not owe for the days she could not return it. The same words cut both ways, depending on which end of the promise you were standing at.

"Force majeure," he said to Mr. Lim, pointing at the heading. "So the reservation doesn't bind you right now."

"That's the size of it," Mr. Lim said. He did not sound sorry, exactly, but he did not sound like a man enjoying the loophole either. He sounded like a man who had explained the same three paragraphs ninety times since six in the morning. "I can put you on the list for whatever comes back today. Liability's the same either way. You sign, you accept the terms."

Here was where the two halves of Seth's brain, which his mother called his lawyer half and his concert half, began to argue. The lawyer half noted that the ticket in his email, the forty-dollar one, probably contained the same words somewhere in its own fine print, and that the storm had probably released the venue too, and that Tessa and Arthur might be sitting in a flooded field learning the same lesson from the other direction. The concert half noted that the storm was, per the radio, drifting east, and that the highway south was officially reopening at noon, and that a man at the counter behind them had just said his brother was driving down regardless, terms or no terms.

"You could call the festival," his mother said, finally pocketing the phone. "Before we decide anything."

"I already did," Seth said. He had, in the bathroom, while she was claiming her arms were full. "The recording says refunds are evaluated case by case under the ticket terms. It doesn't say which way." He was aware, saying it, that this was the honest shape of the thing: a clause that excused everybody, a highway that might open, two friends in a field, and no rule that told you whether to drive toward the promise or away from it. "I think the clause covers them too. But I don't know if the storm counts as preventing the show, or just inconveniencing it."

"Put us on the list," his mother said. "And Seth, whatever you're doing with your face, stop it. You look like you're drafting a memo."

Mr. Lim typed, printed, turned the clipboard around, and offered her the pen. She slid it down the counter to Seth without looking at it.

"Your signature," she said. "You read it. I didn't."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: For the same sample size, a poll's margin of error is largest when opinion is split near 50 percent, and pollsters usually report that largest figure.
story:
The campaign office smelled of burnt coffee and wet cardboard, and Aaron had claimed the corner desk because it had the only outlet that still worked. He was supposed to be calling voters for Mr. Castillo, who was running for the school board, but his chemistry test was on Monday and the flashcards kept migrating back into his hand. Graphite, diamond, fullerene: three allotropes of carbon, same element arranged differently. He was on the card about mass spectrometers, how the machine ionizes atoms so they can be sorted by mass, when Carissa dropped a printout in front of him.

"This came from the pollster," she said. "Castillo wants it up on the wall, but I don't know what to tell people when they ask questions."

The page had two numbers on it. On the question of whether voters had heard of Mr. Castillo, 81 percent said yes. On the question of whether they would vote for him, it was 52 to 48 against his opponent. Underneath both, in small type, it said margin of error plus or minus four points. Aaron read it twice, then a third time, because the same four was attached to both numbers and that seemed careless, like the pollster had copied and pasted without looking. He said so, and Joey, sprawled on the folding chair by the window, gave a blase shrug without lifting his eyes from his phone.

"They're numbers," Joey said. "They're all made up anyway."

Aaron didn't think they were made up. He thought about the 81 percent, which couldn't really be 77 or 85 in any way that mattered, and then the 52, which could easily be 48 if you shook the box. He asked Carissa for the folder the printout had come from, and she dug it out of a milk crate by the copier, and inside, stapled behind the summary page, was a longer report with a paragraph of notes. He read it standing up, one hip against the desk, while rain started ticking against the window.

The notes said that the margin of error wasn't one fixed truth about the poll but a range that depended on how the answers fell, and that it was largest when opinion was split near 50 percent. For the same number of people surveyed, the report said, a lopsided result came with a smaller true margin. But the number printed at the bottom, the plus or minus four, was the largest one, reported for everything, because pollsters gave the worst case rather than a different figure for every question. So the 81 might be tighter than it looked, and the 52 was almost certainly looser, sitting right where the error was fattest.

"Huh," Aaron said, mostly to himself, and Carissa leaned over his shoulder.

"What," she said. "Tell me, because Castillo's going to ask at six and I have to say something that isn't just me panicking."

"It's split down the middle," Aaron said. "That's why the four is the four. It's the biggest it gets, and they just print the biggest one everywhere." He tapped the page. "On the name recognition thing, it's probably less than that. But we don't get to know how much less."

Carissa looked at him, then at the wall where the printout was going to hang, then at the list of undecided voters still waiting to be called. Outside, the rain had thickened, and the evening shift of canvassers was due to leave at six-thirty with their clipboards and cheap ponchos. She rubbed her eyes and said, "So when somebody calls and asks if we're winning, I say it's too close and we keep knocking on doors."

"That's what I'd say," Aaron said.

At six, Mr. Castillo came in shaking water off his jacket, and he read the printout while standing in the doorway, one shoe still on the mat. He was quiet for longer than Aaron expected. Then he asked Carissa for the full call sheet, not just the undecideds, and asked Joey, who had by then put his phone away, whether he could drive two of the older volunteers home if the rain got worse, because they didn't like driving at night. Joey said yes, actually getting up to find the car keys.

Aaron put his flashcards away and pulled the phone list toward him. Graphite and diamond could wait; carbon would still be carbon tomorrow, arranged however it wanted. He dialed the first number, and while it rang he watched Mr. Castillo pull on his own poncho, folding the poll report into his pocket instead of pinning it to the wall. The line clicked open, and a woman's voice said hello.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
Kate got the window seat because she was first on at the far stop, which almost never happened, and she spread her chapter of the novel across her knees before the bus had finished its first turn. Ms. Pritchard's assignment sat half-written in her notebook: choose a critical lens, apply it to the chapter, be prepared to argue it on Monday. She had circled the word Marxist twice and then, in smaller letters, written or feminist, as though the two were pills she could titrate between, a little of each until the essay felt right.

Tegan dropped into the seat across the aisle, and Cory folded himself in beside her, both of them smelling of the chlorine from early swim practice. "Tell me you've started," Tegan said. "Tell me you understand what Pritchard wants, because I've read the chapter three times and all I've got is that the mother is awful."

"She is awful," Kate said. "That's the feminist part, maybe. She marries for security and the whole book punishes her for it." She turned the pages without seeing them, because the honest problem was that she didn't want the easier lens. The feminist reading she could do half-asleep, and doing it felt like handing in something she'd already thought in ninth grade.

Cory leaned over the seat, breath fogging on the cold glass. "Okay, but what's the Marxist one even look like? Everyone keeps saying it and nobody says what you actually do."

"You look at who's doing the work," Kate said slowly, and as she said it she heard how empty it sounded, a fortune cookie. "Like, whose labour makes their comfortable lives possible." She hated saying things she couldn't back up. She pulled the chapter toward her and found a pencil, and because she had no better method, she started counting.

The family in the chapter lived grandly, in a way the prose treated as weather, as atmosphere. Every comfort arrived as if by itself: fires lit, meals carried in, a carriage brought round. Kate began making a small tally in the margin each time a servant was so much as named, a groom, a cook, a maid with the door. It took her two pages to notice the other column was empty. The servants never spoke. She counted again from the top, slower this time, ready to be wrong, and arrived at the same strange arithmetic: eleven names, or near-names, and not one line of speech in the entire chapter.

"Tegan. Look at this." She held the book out across the aisle, margin bristling with pencil strokes. "Count how many times the servants get mentioned, then count how many times any of them actually says anything."

Tegan took it, and her eyes moved, and Cory craned in over her shoulder. The bus swayed through the long suburban stretch where the houses got smaller. "Zero," Tegan said at last. "They're mentioned all over and they never talk. Not once."

"That's it," Kate said, too loud for the empty bus, and lowered her voice. "That's the reading. The novel only mentions them in passing, but they're the ones keeping everybody in candlelight and dinner. The whole comfortable world is standing on them and the book can't even let them finish a sentence." She was writing fast now, the essay assembling itself in fragments, and she could feel the two lenses pressing against each other, because the awful mother was also a woman with no money of her own, trapped in the same machine by a different door. She didn't yet know how to hold both at once without blunting both.

"So which one are you picking?" Cory asked. He had that look he got when he'd decided the question was a trap.

"I don't know," Kate said, and it came out more defiant than she meant. "The Marxist one is the one I found. Nobody handed it to me. But the feminist one is still true too, and I can't just pretend it isn't because it's convenient." She looked at the tally marks, eleven small strokes, and then at the blank space beside them where the voices should have been, and wrote at the bottom of the page: both are true; the chapter is doing two things at once.

The bus slowed for her corner. Tegan handed the book back with the margin still showing, and Kate slid it into her bag without closing the notebook, wanting the pencil marks where she could see them. She stood, gripping the cold rail, and Cory called after her, "Good luck arguing two things at Pritchard."

"You're supposed to argue a considered position," Kate said, stepping down into the blue evening, and behind her the doors hissed shut.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it.
story:
The first day of preseason left Katherine feeling invincible. She had sprinted until her vision whitened at the edges, lodged two goals past the backup keeper, and walked home from the field with her cleats swinging from one finger, certain that this was the year her body would finally cooperate. By Thursday she could barely get down the stairs. Her thighs burned with every step, and when she lowered herself onto the bench beside the equipment shed, she did it in stages, like an old woman easing into a cold bath.

"You look like a haunted chair," said Alexis, dropping down beside her with a water bottle. Practice hadn't even started; they were early, and the field lay empty except for the groundskeeper pushing the mower along the far touchline.

"I felt nothing on Monday," Katherine said. "Not a thing. I did the whole ladder drill twice." She rubbed her quad through her shorts, wincing. "Why is it worse now than it was then?"

Alexis shrugged. Kabir, arriving with a bag of orange slices, overheard them and crouched in the grass. "Delayed-onset muscle soreness," he said. "It peaks twenty-four to seventy-two hours after a hard workout, not right after it."

"Twenty-four to seventy-two," Katherine repeated, filing the numbers away like contraband.

That was the fact she carried home, and it sat with her all evening while she iced her legs on the couch. If the worst of it arrived a day or two later, then the day after a hard session was not a blank slate; it was a debt coming due. Her father asked twice whether she wanted dinner, and twice she said in a minute, because she was drawing a grid on the back of a school handout. Seven columns, one for each day of the week.

The next morning she found Ms. Thompson in the gym office before homeroom. Ms. Thompson coached the junior team and kept a shelf of binders behind her desk, and when Katherine laid out her grid, Ms. Thompson put on her reading glasses and studied it in silence. Hard session Monday. Rest Tuesday, or something light. Skills work Wednesday, when the soreness from Monday should be fading. Hard again Thursday, but not as hard, with a longer warm-up in front of it. Rest Saturday before Sunday's scrimmage.

"You've put the easy day after the hard day," Ms. Thompson observed. "Why?"

"Because I can't feel Monday on Monday," Katherine said. "I feel it Tuesday and Wednesday. So Tuesday has to absorb it." She pointed at the warm-up boxes she had shaded into every column. "And these are longer on the days after the hard sessions, because I'll be stiffer than I think I am."

Ms. Thompson took off the glasses and folded them. "There's a whole zeitgeist around pushing through everything, you know. No days off, grind culture, all of it. It fills my inbox every August." She tapped the two rest days on the grid. "You're arguing against the weather."

"It's not really an argument," Katherine said. "It's just arithmetic. If the soreness peaks later, then rest isn't weakness. It's timing."

She believed that, mostly. But lying in bed that night, she turned the plan over the way she turned over any capricious thing, testing it for cracks. Her body was not a machine that ran on schedules; some weeks it would ache on the second day, some weeks the third, some weeks hardly at all. The plan assumed a pattern her legs had promised but might not keep. She could accept that, she decided. A plan that was honest about its own uncertainty was better than no plan, and better than a plan that pretended to be certain.

Saturday she ran the long warm-up she had written for herself, jogging the perimeter of the empty field while the morning fog burned off the grass. The soreness was almost gone, and her legs felt transfigured, light and new, as though the week of rest had remade them quietly while she wasn't looking. Alexis was already at the far goal, juggling a ball against her knees, and Kabir sat on the bleachers eating the last orange slice. Katherine finished her final stride, checked her watch against the schedule folded in her pocket, and waved.

"Sunday's the scrimmage," Alexis called across the grass. "You ready?"

Katherine tucked the paper away, took the ball Alexis rolled her, and struck it cleanly into the upper corner of the net.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The shelf label's unit price shows the cost per gram, litre or item, which lets shoppers compare packages of different sizes fairly.
story:
Ms. Iyer slapped a photocopied worksheet on the counter beside the industrial stove and said, "Your final project is a week of meals. Planned, shopped, batch-cooked. Yes, Reese, you may survive on instant noodles the rest of your life, but not in my classroom."

Leo read the worksheet twice. Seven dinners, a budget of forty dollars, everything cooked across two lab periods, the portions portioned and labelled like evidence. Beside him, Harley was already sketching a logo for a meal she refused to describe, saying only that it involved eggs and would "change the course of history." Leo felt a smaller, more private pressure: at home his mother worked evenings now, and someone had to figure out what the household ate. He had volunteered without exactly deciding to, the way you sign up for things in a hallway when a teacher looks at you expectantly.

Planning went badly before it went well. He wrote a menu that required saffron, because a video had made saffron seem essential to personhood, and Ms. Iyer circled it with her red pen and wrote "aspirational" in the margin. "You can't commodify your way into being a good cook," she said, tapping his grocery list. "Half the internet wants to sell you the identity along with the spices." Harley leaned over to admire the word commodify, then borrowed it, mispronounced it, and used it about the cafeteria's pretzel supply within the hour. The three of them rebuilt the list around oats, lentils, rice, frozen vegetables, and a whole chicken that would stretch across three nights if Leo didn't flinch at touching it.

Saturday morning the four of them, Leo, Reese, Harley, and Harley's reusable bags, met at the grocery store with the solemnity of an expedition. Ms. Iyer had given them one instruction and a warning: bring receipts, and do not trust your eyes. "Trust them about what?" Reese had asked, but she had only smiled in the way of adults saving a lesson for later, which was annoying, though Leo had to admit it worked on him, because he spent the first ten aisles trying to guess what trap she'd set.

The trap was oatmeal. Leo reached for the big bag, nearly two kilograms, because everyone knew big bags were cheaper, and he was about to drop it in the cart when Harley grabbed his wrist. "Wait. The shelf label thing. Look." Beneath the row of bags, a small white sticker listed a second price, smaller than the first. "Unit price," Harley read. "It's the cost per gram, or per litre, or per item. That's how you compare different sizes." Leo looked from the big bag to the small one beside it and did the shameful arithmetic twice. The larger bag's cost per gram was higher. The big bag, the confident family-size bag, the bag that implied thrift through sheer volume, was more expensive. He put it back with the tenderness one uses to break up with someone.

"Wait," Reese said, holding up the small bag. "So the whole point of the label is you can compare packages of different sizes fairly?" "Apparently," Leo said, still slightly betrayed. They walked the aisles testing it on everything, juice, detergent, canned tomatoes, and it kept being true, and it kept being surprising, as though the shelves had been quietly honest this whole time and nobody had told him. By the dairy case he was reading labels aloud like a person with a new philosophy.

The cooking itself took two days and most of Leo's patience. On Sunday he simmered the chicken with onions until the kitchen windows went diaphanous with steam, the glass fogging so completely that the backyard dissolved into a soft grey suggestion of itself. In English class he had learned the word metonymy that same week, the crown for the queen, the White House for the government, and standing at the stove he thought the pot on the burner was standing in for his whole family getting fed, which he did not say out loud because Harley would never have let him live. Harley and Reese came over with their own grocery hauls and the counter turned into an assembly line: lentils into containers, rice into the fridge, oats, mislabeled by Reese, into a jar marked "lentils," which would be discovered tragically on Thursday morning.

On Monday Leo brought Ms. Iyer his receipts, the meal chart, and a container of soup. She read the receipt with actual attention, then looked up. "So which bag of oats did you buy?" "The small one," Leo said. "The label was right there the whole time. I don't know why I never looked." He paused, because he wanted to be accurate. "I still don't know if my whole plan is good, honestly. Thursday is lentils that might be oats." Ms. Iyer tasted the soup, considered it, and pushed the container back across the counter to him. "Label your jars," she said, "and bring me some anyway."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In France, the directly elected president appoints the prime minister, but the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion.
story:
The invitation had said delegates should arrive at city hall by nine, and Samuel arrived at eight forty, which left him twenty minutes to sit on the cold stone steps and read his notes again. He was representing France in a model summit on government systems, and the problem he could not solve was how to explain a country that seemed to belong to two categories at once. His notes had desiccated somewhere between the library and this morning; the margins had gone dry and curling, the ink faded, and the argument he thought he had built the night before now looked like disconnected phrases.

Ludovik found him there, holding a paper cup of vending machine coffee and looking unhurried in a way that Samuel envied. "You're doing the parliamentary side, right?" Ludovik asked, settling beside him on the steps. "I've got presidential. Gideon drew the comparison round, the lucky one. All he has to do is sit there and say which of us sounds better."

"I've got France," Samuel said. "That's the problem."

"France is parliamentary."

"That's what I thought." He turned the page toward Ludovik, though the handwriting was too cramped to be legible to anyone else. "But it isn't only that. The president is elected directly. By the people. Not by the assembly, the way a prime minister is."

Ludovik squinted at the steps as though the answer might be chalked on them. "So it's presidential."

"It's not only that either." Samuel heard how circular he sounded and disliked it. The whole point of the summit, Mr. Aquino had said at the last briefing, was to give an incisive account, not a hedge. "In a pure presidential system the head of government is elected and can't be removed by the legislature. In a pure parliamentary one the head of government comes out of the assembly and can be brought down by it. France has both moving parts."

They went inside when the doors opened. City hall had been built in a period that could not decide what it was either, Samuel noticed: marble columns in front, plain brick behind, an atrium that belonged to neither century. The summit was held in the council chamber, where the desks formed a horseshoe and someone had left the public microphone switched on, so that every shuffle of paper was faintly amplified overhead.

Gideon was already seated, leaning back with his comparison chart, and he raised two fingers in greeting without straightening up. "France again," he said, when Samuel slid into the seat marked FR. "You've argued with me about France three times this month."

"Because it doesn't fit your chart," Samuel said. "Look. The president is directly elected. The president appoints the prime minister. So far, presidential, or close enough." He set his pen down on the desk, then a second pen beside it, an inch apart. "But the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign. They do it by passing a censure motion. The legislature can bring down the government. That part is parliamentary."

Gideon sat up at last. "Then who actually runs the country?"

"That's what I've been trying to figure out," Samuel admitted. "The president picks the prime minister, but the assembly can push that government out. The two of them are holding the same thing from opposite ends."

When his turn came, Samuel stood at the central lectern and spoke more slowly than he had planned, laying the two systems side by side the way he had laid the pens. A presidential system elects its head of government and keeps the legislature from removing that person. A parliamentary system lets the assembly withdraw its confidence and bring the government down. France, he said, does not sit neatly in either column; it borrows the election from one and the removal from the other. He said it twice, in different words, because the first version had sounded like syntax to him, an arrangement of clauses, and the second sounded like a country.

From the chair, Mr. Aquino asked the question Samuel had been dreading. "So which is better, Mr. Delegate? You've shown us the mechanism. Now tell us your position."

Samuel looked down at his notes, then closed them. "A presidential system protects the head of government from the assembly's moods, but it can protect a government nobody wants. A parliamentary system answers quickly to the assembly, but it can fall too quickly, over one vote. France's arrangement splits those risks between two offices instead of stacking them on one." He paused, aware of Gideon watching him from across the horseshoe. "I can tell you how it works. I can't yet tell you which failure I'd rather live with, and I don't think anyone can without living there."

He carried his notes back to his seat. The chairs in the chamber creaked as delegates shifted; through the tall windows the morning sun had moved onto the marble floor of the atrium, bright on one column, leaving the other in shade. Gideon leaned over the empty desk between them and slid his comparison chart across. In the column marked FRANCE he had drawn, instead of a check mark, two arrows pointing in opposite directions.

"That's your grade, I think," Gideon said. "Arrows. No box."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Brown nitrogen dioxide forms colourless dinitrogen tetroxide in an exothermic reaction, so a sealed tube of the gas turns paler when cooled and darker brown when warmed.
story:
Michael's grandfather kept the chemistry supplies in a cabinet under the stairs, behind the winter coats, and Michael had to exhume the box from beneath a collapsed stack of mothball-scented sweaters before he could even see what he had. The retake was Monday. Ms. Swampy had written "Le Chatelier, again" at the top of his failed quiz, which was either a diagnosis or a small act of pity, and Michael had spent the train ride out to the house on Saturday telling himself that equilibrium was not going to be the thing that kept him out of the university program he wanted.

"Grandpa, do you still have the demo tubes?" he called up the stairs.

His grandfather came down slowly, one hand on the rail, and stood in the hallway in his cardigan, looking at the box Michael had dragged into the light. "Somewhere. I taught gases for thirty years. What you hunting for?"

"The nitrogen dioxide one. Ms. Swampy showed us a video, but the camera work was terrible and I couldn't tell what was happening." This was mostly true. The video had been fine; Michael's attention had been the problem. He was good at memorizing, bad at believing, and somewhere between those two failings the whole unit had slipped through him.

His grandfather moved the sweaters aside himself, found a wooden rack at the bottom, and lifted out a sealed glass tube, fat as a sausage, stoppered and glued shut decades ago. The gas inside was brown, not the warm brown of tea but the malevolent brown of something that seemed to be watching you back. "Careful with it," his grandfather said, though he handed it over without ceremony. "Nitrogen dioxide. Two of those molecules will hold hands and make dinitrogen tetroxide when they get the chance, and the tetroxide is colourless. Sealed tube, so nothing gets in or out. That's the whole trick."

Everett texted while Michael was still holding the tube up to the window: are you actually studying at your grandpas or did you die. Michael typed back, studying, come monday if you want to see my corpse, and then set the phone face-down on the counter because his grandfather had put a kettle on and was watching him with an expression Michael recognized from every awkward family dinner: the look of a man deciding how much to interfere.

"Ms. Swampy said the reaction is exothermic," Michael said. "I wrote that down. I can recite it. But reciting isn't the same as being able to predict anything."

"So predict something."

Michael looked at the kettle, then at the tube in his hand, and felt something assemble itself in his head the way a sentence sometimes does, all at once and slightly before he was ready for it. Exothermic meant the reaction gave off heat, which meant heat behaved like a product, which meant if you cooled the tube the reaction should run forward, toward the colourless stuff, and the gas should turn pale. He said so, out loud, in a voice that surprised him with its certainty.

"Then don't take my word for it," his grandfather said, and filled a bowl from the cold tap, adding ice from the freezer tray he still made by hand. "Your grandmother's table, though. Use the cork mat."

Michael lowered the tube into the ice water and crouched so his eyes were level with the surface. For a moment nothing happened, and he had time to think that he had it backwards, that he was about to watch his own reasoning fail in real time. Then the brown began to leach out of the gas, from the top down, like the colour was being paid out of it, until what remained was a pale amber, almost nothing. He pulled the tube out and wrapped both hands around it, and warmth from his palms crept back in, and the brown returned, darkening steadily, until the tube looked as though someone had cut a section out of a thundercloud. His grandfather said nothing at all, which Michael understood was the highest compliment available.

He wrote it out that night at the kitchen table while his grandfather watched a documentary at low volume: brown nitrogen dioxide, colourless dinitrogen tetroxide, exothermic, so cooling drove it paler and warming drove it darker, and the system answered you by moving, by pushing back against whatever you did to it, without ever finishing, without ever picking a side and stopping. He thought about how much of his studying had been an attempt to make things stop, to pin them like butterflies, and how the tube had refused. It only ever shifted. The equilibrium constant was a kind of promise and the position was a kind of negotiation, and he understood the difference now in a way he could not have put into flashcards, though he was honest enough with himself to admit that some of it was still fog. He could predict the direction. What the system was actually doing down among the molecules, he would take on faith until the professor told him otherwise.

On Sunday, Everett and Oakley took the bus out with a bag of chips and no chemistry books between them, and Michael made them sit at the kitchen table while he ran the demonstration twice more, ice water and then his grandmother's kettle, narrating in the flat determined voice of someone converting panic into performance. Oakley, who wanted to study genetics and knew a lot about visible traits, said the colour was like a phenotype, the outward readout of something invisible happening inside, and Michael said yes, exactly, that was exactly it, and wrote that on the back of his hand because it was better than anything on his notes.

"Show me the prediction part," Everett said, leaning over the tube as it paled in the bowl, ice clicking against the glass. "Say it like you'd say it on the quiz."

Michael dried the tube on a dish towel, and the brown bloomed back into it under the kitchen light. "If you cool it, it goes pale," he said. "If you warm it, it goes dark. Watch." He set his thumb against the glass.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared.
story:
Naomi found the mistake on the second page, and by the third page she had stopped hoping it was a copying error. She was sitting on the floor outside the biology lab, waiting for physiology to start, with Freya's homework spread across her knees because Freya had shoved it at her in the hallway and said, "Check it, check it fast, Rodríguez collects it at three." The problem was the same everywhere. For the derivative of x cubed, Freya had written three x cubed, and for x to the fourth she had written four x to the fourth, all the way down the sheet, tidy and confident and wrong.

"Freya. You lowered the coefficient but you left the power alone."

Freya dropped down beside her, close enough that Naomi could smell the cafeteria coffee on her. "What do you mean, left it alone?"

"I mean every single answer." Naomi tapped the page. "Derivative of x cubed is three x squared. The power comes down with the front number and then it drops by one. You did the coming-down part. You forgot the dropping."

Freya took the sheet back and stared at it as though it had betrayed her personally. "That's the power rule?"

"That's the power rule," Naomi said, though an hour ago she hadn't been sure herself. She had transcribed the rule onto an index card last night, word for word from the textbook, and only this morning, checking it against the worked examples, had she understood what the words were doing.

The hallway thinned as the physiology students filed in. Freya wasn't moving. "If I fix these, I get the maxima right too?"

"You don't have the maxima right now. Look." Naomi flipped to the last problem, the one Ms. Rodríguez had designed for Friday's quiz, the polynomial that modeled the height of something over time, a rocket or a thrown ball, Naomi could never remember which.
