"You set your derivative equal to zero and solved. But you solved the wrong derivative. Your answer isn't the peak. It's not anything."

"That's dramatic."

"It's math. It's the opposite of dramatic. It just sits there being wrong."

Freya laughed, which surprised Naomi, because she had braced for defensiveness. Freya had a way of absorbing bad news that made it look like a gift, and Naomi, who tended to hoard her own failures for weeks, had never decided whether she envied this or distrusted it. "Okay," Freya said. "Teach me the dropping thing. Two minutes. Rodríguez is munificent with partial credit but she is not merciful about wrong answers."

Inside the classroom, Ms. Rodríguez was writing the word homeostasis on the board in her slanted, hurried hand. Freya spread the homework on the desk and rewrote the first derivative in pencil, muttering. "Three x squared. Three x squared. Why do I keep wanting to keep the three?"

"Because it feels like the exponent belongs to the number," Naomi said. "Like you're only borrowing it." She had thought about this on the bus that morning, watching the power lines dip and rise between poles, and she still wasn't certain the feeling was wrong so much as it was incomplete. The rule was the rule; why it felt like theft she couldn't say.

"Orion!" Freya called across the room, reckless as always. Orion detangled himself from his bag and leaned over their desks. "Derivative of x cubed. Say it fast."

"Three x squared," he said without hesitation. Then, suspicious: "Why?"

"Naomi's grading me."

Orion looked at the paper, then at Naomi, and something in his face suggested he had made the same mistake once and paid for it. "Set it to zero afterward," he said. "The peak is where the slope quits." He went back to his seat, which was how Orion participated in most things, arriving, contributing a line, vanishing.

Ms. Rodríguez turned from the board. She had the collected look of someone who heard everything and chose, mostly, not to act on it. "Freya, if you're finished tutoring, perhaps you could tell us what the body does when it gets too warm."

"It sweats," Freya said. "It drops the temperature by one."

The class laughed. Ms. Rodríguez closed her eyes for a moment, the way teachers do when a joke is almost accurate, and wrote sweating on the board without comment.

Freya bent back over the homework under cover of the lecture, pencil moving, and at the end of the last problem she circled a number twice and slid the page toward Naomi. The rocket reached its peak at x equals two. Naomi checked it against her own solution from last night and found they matched, digit for digit, and she sat with the small strange pleasure of two people arriving at the same summit by different trails.

"So I get to keep my scholarship math grade," Freya whispered, "and you get to be right, which I know is your favorite thing in the world."

"It's in the top five," Naomi said, and handed the page back.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: At the top of its path a projectile's vertical velocity is zero, but its horizontal velocity is not, so it is still moving.
story:
The playground was empty by six except for the three of them and the long shadow of the slide, and Liam stood at the edge of the wood chips holding a basketball he had no intention of shooting. Claudia had the printout folded in her back pocket, the one with his grade on it, and she kept not mentioning it, which was worse than mentioning it. Sterling arrived last, carrying his phone in both hands like a waiter carrying soup.

"Okay," Sterling said. "Show him."

"Show me what?" Liam said.

"The video I took in fifth period."

He had filmed Mr. Otieno's demonstration from the back row, where he always sat with his hood up, and Liam had assumed at the time that Sterling was doing what Sterling usually did, which was nothing in a documented fashion. But when Sterling held the phone out and Liam watched the small bright screen, he saw the ball leave Mr. Otieno's hand and rise, frame by frame, hang, and fall, and he saw something he had not seen live and had definitely not written on his quiz.

Liam had written, in pencil, then pressed hard enough to emboss the next page, that at the top of its path the ball stops. All of it stops, he had written, before going still for one instant. He had gotten the rest of the problem right, the angle, the components, the arithmetic Mr. Otieno had called tidy, and he had lost almost everything on that single sentence, and the retake was tomorrow morning at 7:40, and if he did not raise the grade he would not be eligible for Friday's meet, and he had told the coach he would be there. He had told her that on Monday, before the quiz, back when the sentence was still something he believed.

"Run it again," Liam said. "Slower."

Sterling scrubbed the video back with his thumb. The ball climbed. Near the peak it seemed, for a handful of frames, to be doing nothing, a gray sphere against the gray doorframe of the gym, and Liam felt the old certainty rise with it, the feeling that obviously the thing pauses, everything pauses at the top, that's what a top is. But Sterling had zoomed in on the edit, and the doorframe had a scuff mark on it, a pale diagonal scrape, and the ball, in every single frame, was sliding sideways past that scrape. It was never in the same place twice.

"It's moving," Liam said. "At the top. It's still moving."

"That's what I said," Sterling said.

"No, you said I was wrong. That's different."

Claudia sat down on the bottom of the slide, which put her at roughly Liam's height for once, and pulled the printout out of her pocket but didn't unfold it. "So say it the way he wants it," she said. "The whole thing, not the shortcut."

Liam looked at the basketball in his hands. He was, by his own account, an autodidact, meaning he had taught himself guitar from videos and chess from a library book and how to ollie from a kid at this same playground two summers ago, and he liked to believe that everything worth knowing could be gotten that way, alone, at night, with the material in front of you. But the material in front of him now was a ball and the sky above the monkey bars, and the sky was refusing to have frames.

"Vertical and horizontal," he said slowly. "They're not the same thing. They don't even know about each other." He bounced the ball once, caught it. "At the top the vertical part, the up part, that's zero. That's gone. But the sideways part isn't. The sideways part just keeps going the whole time."

Claudia unfolded the printout and held it up, and the wind tried to take it, and she pinned it against her knee. His sentence was circled in red, twice, and beside it Mr. Otieno had written one word, "Re-watch," which Liam had taken as an instruction he couldn't follow because the demonstration was over, class was over, the moment had happened once and gone. It had not occurred to him until tonight that moments could be recorded by other people, by Sterling, by anyone, that the world was full of evidence if you weren't too proud to stand where the strange quiet kid was standing.

"Prove it, then," Claudia said, nodding at the court behind the swings, where the rim was bent slightly left and the paint of the key had worn down to gray ellipses. "Not to me. To yourself, before 7:40, or you'll write the same sentence with more confidence."

Liam walked to the foul line. He picked up a piece of chalk someone had left by the fence and drew two arrows on the blacktop, one pointing up and one pointing sideways, delimiting the two directions so cleanly that even he couldn't blend them back together. Then he shot. He shot until his arms ached, and each time the ball rose he said it out loud, "zero up, still sideways," and each time the ball came down through or near the hoop, and the hoop itself was proof, because if the ball truly stopped at the top it would come straight down like a dropped stone, and nothing he had ever shot had come straight down, and he had shot this particular bent rim a thousand times without once letting himself notice that.

Sterling filmed the last shot, the one Liam put up from behind the line with his legs shaking and the streetlight buzzing on. In the video the ball hung at the top of its arc against the basketball standard's straight steel edge, and the edge ran like a ruler behind it, and the ball crawled along that ruler even at the very peak, sideways, patient, unstoppable by gravity which only owned the other direction. Liam watched it four times.

"You going to show him this?" Sterling asked, meaning Mr. Otieno, meaning 7:40, meaning tomorrow.

"He said re-watch," Liam said. He was already drafting the sentence in his head, but what he said out loud, picking up the ball and tucking it under his arm, was, "I'm going to bring my own chalk."

Claudia laughed, and the streetlight flickered, and somewhere past the fence a car went by with its windows down.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
The last Sunday in January found Henry wedged between the arm of Ms. Byrne's couch and a plate of nachos that had gone cold an hour ago. Ms. Byrne had opened her house to the whole block because her television was the largest, and so Henry's father was shouting at the screen from a folding chair, Sophie had claimed the good spot on the rug, and Henry's grandfather sat by the window with a glass of cider he wasn't drinking, watching the game the way you watch weather.

"It wasn't like this in the beginning," his grandfather said during a commercial. "The very first one, I was there. January of sixty-seven. Cold enough to crack the seats. Green Bay. Snow coming sideways off the lake, and we watched the whole thing with our collars up like a bunch of monks."

Sophie sat up. She was at work on a project for Ms. Byrne's class, something about how families keep their past, and she had been trailing Henry's grandfather all afternoon with her phone held low, recording. "You were at the first Super Bowl?" she said. "Actually there?"

"I drove up with two friends from college. Nobody called it the Super Bowl then, but that's what it was."

Henry felt the shape of the story before he felt the problem with it. His grandfather talked about the old days the way other people talked about the weather, generously and without checking, and usually Henry let it go. But Sophie had her phone out, and Sophie's project was going to be graded, and somewhere in the back of his mind a date was misbehaving. He pulled his own phone below the table's edge and typed with his thumb.

The screen was patient with him. The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers had beaten the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10. In Los Angeles. He read it twice, then a third time, because a fact like that has a way of rearranging a room. Los Angeles. There was no snow coming sideways off any lake, unless the lake was imaginary, and his grandfather, who would have been nineteen that winter, had either misremembered an entire afternoon or invented it.

Henry looked at his grandfather's profile against the window, at Sophie's phone tilted like a small black flower toward the story, and did the arithmetic he always did in these moments: the truth against the telling. He could let the recording stand and the wrongness would travel into Sophie's project, into a grade, into the world. Or he could correct an old man in front of a room full of neighbors on the one afternoon of the month that belonged to him.

"Pap," he said, and his voice came out lower than he intended. "The first one wasn't in Green Bay. It was in Los Angeles. January fifteenth, nineteen sixty-seven. Packers over the Chiefs, thirty-five to ten."

The room didn't go silent exactly, but the volume of it changed. His father turned halfway around in the folding chair. Sophie lowered her phone.

His grandfather looked at Henry for a long moment, and Henry braced himself for the wall that older men build around their own histories. Instead the old man laughed, a short, deflated sound, and set down the cider he hadn't been drinking.

"Los Angeles," he said. "Of course it was. I watched it on a television in a bar in L.A., if you want the whole of it, because I was stationed in California that winter and the bar had a color set and my two friends from Wisconsin wrote me letters about the snow at home." He shook his head slowly. "Forty years I've been putting that snow in the stadium. A man starts out remembering a bar and ends up remembering a blizzard."

Sophie was scribbling now, and when Henry caught her eye she mouthed, this is the project. She had been hunting all week for a story that could instantiate her whole argument, that memory isn't a recording but a document that gets edited every time it's read, and here it was, handed over with the nachos. She was sanguine about her grade in a way that made Henry feel, unexpectedly, like something had been taken from him.

Because here was the part he couldn't get straight, even later, walking home across Ms. Byrne's brown savanna of a lawn under the porch lights: his grandfather had thanked him. Clapped him once on the shoulder and said, "Somebody in this family ought to keep the books," as if being corrected were a kind of inheritance. Henry had wanted to defend the truth and instead he had strengthened the story, and he honestly did not know which of those he had done.

At the door his grandfather paused, holding his coat half on.

"Thirty-five to ten," he said. "That part I never got wrong. Write that down, Sophie."

Sophie already had.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
Jordan had pushed the coffee table against the wall and taped a rectangle of masking tape on the carpet to mark the edge of an imaginary stage, and by Saturday afternoon his living room had become a theater with a sofa for an audience. Henry and Ludovik stood inside the tape line holding their scripts, waiting for him to say something. The play was a one-act about two brothers dividing their dead father's belongings, ten minutes long, chosen because it needed only two actors and one room. Jordan had directed nothing in his life. He had watched Mr. Goh run the drama club for four years, standing in the back of the auditorium with his arms crossed, and he had thought, incorrectly, that the job mostly consisted of standing in the back with your arms crossed.

"Okay," he said. "Henry, when you say the line about the affidavit, cross to the chair. Ludovik, stay where you are." He had spent two nights drawing arrows in the margins of his script, tiny maps of intention, and he was proud of them in the way you are proud of something no one has tested yet.

They ran the first scene. Henry delivered the line, "You kept the affidavit, you knew what he was hiding," and walked toward the window instead of the chair, which put him behind Ludovik, which put his back to the sofa, which meant that if an audience had been sitting there it would have seen a shoulder and nothing else.

"Stop," Jordan said. "Not that way. Left. Go left."

Henry went left, which was the window again, and Jordan felt the small hot flare of someone who suspects the fault is not entirely the other person's. "Other left," he said, and Henry stopped, and there was a silence in which everyone understood that Jordan did not actually know which left he meant.

"From where?" Henry asked. He was not being difficult. He was asking the only reasonable question.

Jordan got down on his knees on the carpet and looked at the stage from Henry's position, facing the sofa. He pointed to the chair, which stood to his own right. Then he walked around and sat on the sofa and looked at the stage the way an audience would, and the chair was on the left. He sat there for a moment with the strange vertigo of it, the same room reversed, as if he had walked into a photograph of the living room printed backward.

"Stage left is the actor's left," he said slowly, working it out as he said it. "Facing the audience. So it's the opposite of what the audience calls left." He stood up. "From now on I'll say stage left or stage right, and it's from your point of view, facing us."

"So when you said left just now," Ludovik said, "you meant audience left, which is stage right, which is the chair."

"Yes," Jordan said. "Sorry. Yes."

They ran it again, and this time Henry crossed to the chair on the correct side and the scene opened up, and Jordan began to understand what the arrows in his margins were actually for. It was not command. It was sightlines, geometry, the plain fact that two hundred people would watch this from one direction only, and every choice had to answer to that single, fixed eye.

The rehearsal was not smooth after that. It was less bad, in stages. Ludovik kept drifting upstage when he got emotional, retreating into the corner by the bookshelf as though the argument itself were pushing him there, and Jordan had to decide whether that instinct was wrong or whether it was the most honest thing in the scene. Mr. Goh, when Jordan had asked him in September how to direct, had said only, "Protect the actor's instinct and the audience's attention, and figure out which one you're betraying." Jordan had thought it was a joke. He now thought it was an affidavit of some kind, a signed statement of what the job cost.

He tried telling Ludovik to hold his ground at the crucial line, "You always take everything," and Ludovik did, and the moment flattened and died. He tried letting Ludovik retreat, and the moment lived but got small, swallowed by the corner. On the fifth run Jordan stopped everything and said, "What if Henry follows you? You retreat, he advances, and you end up against the bookshelf with him standing over you." Ludovik looked at Henry. Henry shrugged. They tried it, and the room changed temperature, and all three of them knew it, and nobody said anything for a second because saying something would have broken it.

At seven o'clock the mother called from the kitchen that there was food, and the actors collapsed onto the sofa, and Jordan sat on the pushed-back coffee table facing them. He had been hard on them somewhere in the fourth hour; there had been a moment when he'd said something close to vitriolic about wasted time, and he was still ashamed of it in the low, useful way that shame tells you who you nearly became. Directing was not standing at the back with crossed arms. It was standing between two ways of seeing a single room, the actor's and the audience's, and translating, and being translated, and being wrong in both directions until something held.

He did not know yet whether the play would be good. He knew the crossing to the chair worked, and the pursuit into the bookshelf worked, and he knew that by next week the actors would have habituated themselves to the stage directions so thoroughly that the words "stage left" would move their bodies before their minds caught up, which was the whole strange point of rehearsal. Everything else, the pacing, the ending, whether an audience would feel what he felt in his own living room at 6:52 on a Saturday, stayed uncertain, and he decided he could carry that.

"Ludovik," he said, standing, pulling the masking tape roll from his pocket. "Tomorrow we tape the bookshelf. And when you take everything, you go stage left. Say it back to me."

"Stage left," Ludovik said, and stepped, without looking down, exactly where the tape would be.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States.
story:
The movers left at four, and after they pulled away the street went so quiet that Brandon could hear his own footsteps on the porch. The new house smelled like paint and cardboard, and his room was delimited by stacks of boxes he had labeled in a hurry: CLOTHES, MISC, MISC AGAIN. Somewhere down the block a sprinkler ticked, and a girl about his age was dragging a recycling bin to the curb in sock feet. He went inside before she could look up.

His mother had said the move would be good for them, and maybe it would, but that word, good, seemed to delimit nothing. It didn't say what it was good for, or what it cost. Back home, Mariah had promised they'd talk every day, and Chanel had promised nothing, which somehow felt more honest. In the two weeks since the truck was packed, he and Mariah had traded maybe six texts, each one smaller than the last, like coins worn smooth.

He sat on the floor of his empty room with his phone and found an article he'd half-read in the car, something his father had put on the dash for him. In May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy had issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States. He read the sentence twice. An advisory. Even loneliness came with paperwork now.

Outside, a screen door banged. The sock-feet girl was standing at the foot of his driveway holding a foil-covered dish, and when he opened the front door she held it up like a badge. "My mom made too much lasagna," she said. "I'm Chanel. You're the people from the truck."

"I'm Brandon." He took the dish, which was warm, and for a second the whole gesture felt like artifice, a neighborhood performance of welcome that would evaporate the moment the foil came off. But her socks had a hole in one toe, which for some reason made it harder to distrust her.

"You looked like a prisoner on that porch," she said. "You were doing the stare-at-nothing thing."

"I was going to call somebody."

"Call them," she said. "Seriously. Haven't you heard? The Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, put out an advisory in May 2023 saying loneliness and isolation are an epidemic in the United States. Like an actual epidemic." She said it the way she might have recited a fact from a quiz she'd barely studied for, and then shrugged. "That's what my mom keeps quoting at me since we moved here last year."

He laughed before he could decide whether to. "That's the second time today I've heard that."

"Then it's a sign," Chanel said, and pointed at his phone. "Go on. I'll wait, but not weirdly. I'll water nothing in the yard."

He sat on the porch steps and called Mariah, and she picked up on the second ring. That was the good part. The bad part came right behind it: music, voices, somebody yelling her name from another room. "Brandon! Hold on, I can't really, we're at Dara's," she said, and Dara was a name he didn't know, a name that hadn't existed in his life three weeks ago. "Can I call you tomorrow?" Her voice was kind, which made it worse, and he said sure, sure, and she was gone in eleven seconds by the clock on his phone.

He stayed on the steps for a while. He had wanted the advisory to mean something simple, that calling was medicine, that one call would close the distance like a bridge sliding into place. Instead the call had shown him the distance was real, that other lives kept moving, seismic in their own small ways, whether he was there or not. And yet Mariah had picked up. She had said tomorrow. Both things were true at once and he couldn't make them into one clean feeling.

Chanel had settled cross-legged on his lawn, pretending to pull weeds. "Bad call?" she asked.

"Not bad," he said. "Just short. There were people at her house." He turned the foil dish over in his hands. "My friend Chanel, back home, would say that means she's fine."

"Is she?" Chanel asked.

"I don't know. Maybe that's the point. Maybe she's fine and lonely at the same time, and I can't know which from here." He stood up. "Do you want to come in? We have plates somewhere. We have lasagna, apparently."

She brushed grass off her knees and followed him up the steps, and at the door he set the dish on the railing and, before he could talk himself out of it, opened his phone and typed to Mariah: call me tomorrow, even if it's short. Then he held the door.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The United States baby boom generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and its bulge on the pyramid has now moved into the retirement ages.
story:
The printer at the public library took forty seconds to cough out Mason's population pyramid, and he spent most of them watching the tray like it owed him something. The chart showed the United States, ages stacked in bars, males on the left, females on the right. Ms. Cho had written the assignment on the board in her narrow hand: analyse the structure and predict whether the country will need more schools or more nursing homes. Two paragraphs, due tomorrow. Mason had one paragraph and a grandmother who had moved into Fernwood Court eleven days ago.

He spread the printout across the table by the window. Mekhi sat across from him with his own pyramid, Nigeria's, wide at the base and tapering fast, a Christmas tree of a country. Mekhi kept tapping his pencil against it.

"Mine's easy," Mekhi said. "All the kids. Schools everywhere. Yours just goes out in the middle like somebody squeezed it."

Mason traced the bars with his finger. The pyramid didn't look like a pyramid at all. It narrowed at the bottom, pinched in the middle, and then swelled out around the ages sixty to eighty before thinning again at the top. The bulge was unmistakable once you saw it, a fat band sitting in the retirement ages like a crowd that had moved through a stadium and settled in one section of seats.

"My grandpa keeps saying his whole generation showed up at once," Mason said. "Him and Grandma, all their friends, same years. Nineteen forty-six to sixty-four." He said the years because they were printed on the sheet Ms. Cho had handed out, a footnote he'd read twice. He looked at where those years would land on the pyramid now. The bulge. The whole bulge. His grandmother wasn't an exception to the chart; she was the chart.

Karlee slid into the third chair with a coffee she wasn't supposed to have in the library. "Whose is that?"

"USA." Mason turned the paper toward her.

"Looks lugubrious," she said. "All that weight at the top."

"It's not at the top. It's at sixty and up." He set the sheet down flat. "Retirement ages. And it's not sad, it's just, they're all there at the same time."

The reference desk was three aisles away, and Mason had been avoiding it for half an hour because the librarian was Ms. Cho's friend and he didn't want word getting back that he couldn't do the analysis. But he couldn't make his second paragraph say anything except "nursing homes, probably," which Ms. Cho would circle in red and write "Support this" beside. So he walked over and asked for the statistical abstract, and the librarian found him a bigger pyramid, one from a decade ago, printed larger so the ages were labelled bar by bar.

He carried it back and laid it beside the first one. Karlee leaned in. "Why are they different shapes?"

"That's the same country," Mekhi said, squinting. "It just moved."

It had moved. In the older chart the bulge sat lower, in the working ages, and in the newer one it had climbed into the retirement ages, as if a decade had carried it upward like a slow elevator. Mason checked the footnote again, 1946 to 1964, did the arithmetic in the margin of his notebook, and put his pencil down. The generation had been born in those years and its bulge on the pyramid had now moved into the retirement ages. That was the whole answer. Not a guess. A thing you could point at.

"So write it," Mekhi said. "Nursing homes. Done. Let's go, I'm hungry."

"It's not done." Mason pulled the sheet back before Mekhi could stack it. "Because my dad keeps saying she'll be home by spring. Fernwood's just temporary, rehab for her hip. But I went Sunday and the hallway had a piano in it and a bulletin board with a September activities calendar. They don't put up September calendars for people leaving in spring."

Karlee said nothing for a moment. The piano reference had landed somewhere. "What are you going to write in the paragraph, then?"

Mason looked at the two pyramids side by side. The assignment asked for a prediction, one need or the other, schools or nursing homes, as though a country could want only one thing at a time. His first paragraph had tried to sound certain, the way Ms. Cho's rubric liked, a claim and two supports and a clinching sentence. He'd been inculcated in that form since seventh grade, claim, evidence, so what, and the form had always fit him like a uniform. But the so what kept splitting on him tonight. Fernwood needed aides and a piano player and someone to read the activities calendar aloud to his grandmother, whose glasses had gone missing in the move. The elementary school four blocks from his house had just cut a music teacher. Both of those things were true and the pyramid held both of them in the same fat band.

He started the second paragraph over. He wrote that the country would need the nursing homes first, that the bulge in the retirement ages made that immediate, and that the schools question depended on what the bars under age twenty did next, which the chart showed but did not settle. He wrote the word "probably" and left it in. Ms. Cho might circle it. He looked at the word and left it anyway, because his father said spring and the September calendar said otherwise and somewhere between the two of them was a truth shaped like a bar on a graph, wide and gray and honest about nothing except its own size.

Mekhi was packing his bag. "You're seriously leaving 'probably' in there?"

"It's what I actually know," Mason said.

Karlee drank her coffee. "You're going to visit her Sunday?"

The library speakers chimed the fifteen-minute warning. Mason folded the older pyramid and put it in his notebook, the one with the bulge halfway up, so his grandmother would be in the middle of the page when he showed her. She liked knowing where she stood. "I'm going Sunday," he said. "And I'm bringing this."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
story:
The library had claimed its chairs by mid-afternoon, and Jackson spread his debate notes across the last free table, weighing the corners down with a copy of a thin book on jurisprudence he'd pulled from the shelf an hour ago. In two days he and Keith would argue against mandatory minimum sentences in front of a panel that included a sitting judge, and Jackson wanted the case to be airtight, or at least honest, which he was beginning to suspect were not the same thing.

"So I go second," Keith said, tapping the affirmative case they'd sketched the night before. "And I hit them with this: if we let judges decide sentences one by one, we get bias. Same crime, two neighborhoods, two totally different punishments. That's why rules exist."

"That's not what they're saying, though." Nicola had arrived quietly, the way she did, and set down two coffees, sliding one toward Keith before Jackson even asked. She nodded at the opposing briefs scattered across the table. "They're saying mandatory minimums incapacitate judges from considering context. They never said no rules at all."

Keith frowned at his own notes. "Fine, then they should have said that."

"They did say that," Jackson said, and turned the page so Keith could see the highlighted line. "Page three. It's the first thing they argue." He read it aloud, the part about discretion within guidelines, and watched Keith's shoulders settle a little, the way they did when he stopped defending and started listening.

"Okay, but when I practice against them, all they'll do is call me soft on crime," Keith said. "Happens every round."

"Then don't do the same thing back." Jackson pulled out a fresh card. "My coach used to call it a straw man," he said, writing the words at the top. "You build a weaker version of their argument, knock it down, and act like you knocked down theirs. It feels like winning. It's just missing." He'd learned it the hard way last spring, in a round he'd swaggered through, only to watch the ballot: the judge had written, in glacial, unhurried handwriting, that he had answered a claim no one made.

They rebuilt the case that afternoon, paragraph by paragraph. Where the affirmative brief argued for guidelines plus discretion, Jackson drafted a response to that position, not to the imaginary one that was easier to beat. Twice he caught himself drifting, once when he wrote "they want no sentencing rules at all," and he crossed it out so hard the pen tore the card. Nicola, reading over his shoulder, quietly slid the original brief closer so he could check the actual wording against what he remembered.

The harder part came after Keith left for practice. Jackson sat alone with the opposing case and found he could not dismiss it. If discretion produced bias, and guidelines produced rigidity, then any system he defended carried one of those costs, and he could not prove which cost mattered more. He wrote that down too, at the bottom of his final card, in smaller letters: maybe the answer depends on facts about particular courts, facts he didn't have.

Mr. Hernández appeared at the table near closing, gathering stray books onto his cart, and paused over the jurisprudence volume. "You're the one who keeps signing this out," he said. "There's a better chapter in the thick one, shelf behind you, green spine. Nobody's touched it in years." He set it beside Jackson's notes and moved on without waiting for thanks.

Jackson opened it under the reading lamp, found the chapter, and began copying a passage into the card where he'd admitted the uncertainty. Down the long table, Nicola was still there, waiting for him with her coat on, holding the door with one foot. "Bring it," she said. "You can read me the boring part in the car."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area between two curves is found by integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they are ordered that way.
story:
I have always been good at math, which is why it was strange that Tuesday afternoon in the school library I was staring at two answers that could not both be right. My answer was one of them. I want that on the record.

Ryley had spread her work across the long table by the windows, where the afternoon light made the graph paper look almost golden, and Marc-Antoine sat across from her with his arms crossed like a man defending a house. We were the only three left from math club, plus Ms. Farah-Ali at the front desk, stamping returns with a sound like a small door closing. The problem was the area trapped between a line and a parabola. Simple, I'd thought. I'd finished it in ten minutes and then spent twenty checking my hair in the darkened screen of my calculator, because I am, as established, good at math.

"It's three," Ryley said, tapping her paper.

"It's negative three," Marc-Antoine said. "I did it twice."

You could not malign his method, honestly; every integral on his page was flawless, each antiderivative a tidy little machine. He was, in a way, the most diligent acolyte in the room, copying the ritual perfectly without once asking what the ritual was for. I say this with affection. I had produced three as well, or something close to it, though at that point I mostly wanted the whole thing to be someone else's fault, ideally the textbook's.

"Negative area," Ryley said slowly, chewing the cap of her pen. "Can area be negative?"

The library smelled like old carpet and the lemon spray somebody used on it, and I remember thinking that a negative amount of lemon would be a very different room. Then Marc-Antoine slid his page toward me, and I slid mine toward him, and there it was. He had subtracted the parabola from the line. I had subtracted the line from the parabola. Same interval, same curves, opposite results, and neither of us had looked at the picture at all.

I drew the graph again, properly this time, pressing hard enough that the pen nearly went through. Over the interval we were given, the parabola sat above the line, the whole way across. That was the thing I had skipped. You integrate the upper function minus the lower function, over the interval where they're ordered that way, I said, mostly to myself, and Ryley looked up like I'd said something in a language she half remembered. "Upper minus lower," she repeated, and started erasing.

Here is where I have to be honest, or as honest as I get. For a second I wanted to pretend I had known it all along, that the graph was a formality, and I nearly said so. But the truth was I had trusted algebra over geometry, my symbols over my eyes, and the eyes had been right. It was a little humbling. It was also, and I don't think I'm exaggerating, beautiful: the two ways of thinking, the arithmetic and the picture, snapping together like the halves of something that had been waiting on the table the whole time. Ryley got three. Marc-Antoine, muttering that the method was impermeable to criticism, crossed out one subtraction, wrote the other, and got three too.

Ms. Farah-Ali wandered over on her way to the shelves, looked at our three matching answers, and said nothing at all, which was either excellent teaching or simple indifference, and I've never decided which. What I still haven't decided, walking home with my calculator warm in my pocket, is whether the math was telling me the curves had to be ordered that way, or whether I was the one deciding, choosing which sat on top, and the math was just agreeing to my arrangement. Somewhere in there the parabola dipped below the line, outside our interval, and I wondered what happened there, whether you could still call either one the upper one, whether the picture ever stops being about choice.

Ryley stuck her head around a shelf before she left. "Same time Thursday?" she said. "I'm bringing the one with the absolute value in it."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: A credit card's grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month.
story:
The envelope sat between Kate's elbows and the salt shaker, thinner than she expected a first credit card bill to be. She had opened it at the kitchen table because her mother was still at work and the table was where money got handled in their house, usually in the form of receipts smoothed flat and a calculator with a cracked screen. The number at the top said she owed $412. The number in the box that said Minimum Payment Due said $25. She read both twice, then slid the paper closer, as if distance had been the problem.

The card had seemed like a simple thing three weeks ago. Textbooks for the fall semester at the community college, a parking permit, a pair of shoes that did not have a hole in the sole. Her mother had said get one but pay it off every month, and Kate had said yes the way she said most things to her mother, quickly, already thinking about something else. Now the something else was this table, this envelope, and the $310 still sitting in her savings account from two summers of scooping ice cream.

She texted Elyse first, because Elyse had cardiology of the wallet down, receipts filed by month. "Bills here. 412. min is 25."

Elyse called instead of texting back, which meant she was walking somewhere. "Pay the whole thing," she said, before Kate had even said hello. "If you can. My dad made me do the math on mine when I turned eighteen."

"I can, technically." Kate turned the bill over. On the back, in type so small she had to hold it under the lamp, she found the sentence: no interest charged on purchases if the full balance is paid by the due date each month. She read it aloud. "So if I pay it all, they charge me nothing?"

"That's the grace period," Elyse said. "Pay it all every month and it stays free. Pay part and it doesn't."

Kate wrote $412 on the back of the envelope and under it $310, and looked at the gap. The savings account was supposed to be her cushion for the semester, the thing that stood between her and asking her mother, whose own cushion had a congenital thinness that no amount of overtime ever seemed to fatten. If she emptied it to pay the card, she was safe from interest and broke at the same time.

Cade came over at seven with his headphones around his neck, because he had promised to help her move her desk to the apartment she was sharing with Elyse in August, and the desk was still in the garage. He found her at the kitchen table with the bill, the calculator, and two glasses of water she had poured and not touched. He picked up the envelope and read the back. "Twenty-five dollars, man. That's like nothing."

"If I pay twenty-five," Kate said, "they charge interest on the rest. And next month it's more, and it keeps going like that. Elyse says interest is what makes borrowed money cost more the longer you take."

"Then don't borrow." He set the envelope down. "You have the money, don't you?"

"Some."

Cade had a way of looking at a problem as if it were a door that only he knew was unlocked. He was the first of their friends to abscond from a group project senior year, vanishing for three days and returning with a finished poster and no explanation, and Kate had watched him get away with it and felt something complicated about that. She did not want to be his acolyte on money. She said, "It's not that simple. The three hundred in savings is for the whole semester. If I hand it over now, I'm at zero in September."

"So you're choosing between owing them later and having nothing now." He drank one of her untouched glasses of water. "That's the actual choice."

She knew he was right about the shape of it, which annoyed her, and she spread the bill flat again to avoid saying so. The due date was the twenty-eighth. Her next paycheck from the ice cream stand was the thirtieth, two days late, forty hours at eleven dollars an hour, some of which was already spoken for by gas. If she paid the full $412 now, the savings would sit at negative territory she couldn't look at directly. If she paid $25, the balance would grow teeth.

Mr. Goldberg from next door knocked at eight, holding a package that had been delivered to his porch by mistake, her mother's name on the label. Kate took it at the door and then, because he asked what was new, heard herself telling him about the card. He was retired from something no one had ever established, and he had a habit of standing on the back step like a man waiting for a bus. He didn't explain anything. He only said, "My wife paid ours in full for forty years. Never paid them a cent more than the sticker price." Then he pointed at the package. "Tell your mother the box got wet on one corner. It's fine, but she'll want to know."

Kate sat back down and looked at the two numbers she'd written. She thought about the forty years, about Elyse's filed receipts, about her mother smoothing the receipts flat at this same table. Then she took out her phone and moved $25 from savings to checking, and after that, before she could change her mind, moved $25 more, and more, watching the savings number fall until the checking number rose past $412. She left eleven dollars behind, a strange deliberate remainder. She scheduled the payment for the full balance, due on the twenty-eighth, and then called the ice cream stand and asked for extra hours before the semester started.

The manager said she'd check the schedule and call back. Kate set the phone face down on the bill and carried Mr. Goldberg's wet-cornered package to the counter, where her mother would see it first thing.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In his 1979 book The Imperative of Responsibility, Hans Jonas proposed the rule: 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life.'
story:
Simon had volunteered at Hôpital Sainte-Anne for one reason, which was that the form said the shifts were four hours, and it turned out they were four hours long every time, an interminable circuit of corridors that smelled of floor wax and something faintly like pears. He told everyone at school it was for his application. This was mostly true. The rest of it, the part he did not mention, was that his grandmother had died in a hospital exactly like this one the previous March, and he had not visited her in the last week because he had a calculus test, and calculus had gone fine.

On Thursday evenings he delivered things. Flowers, mostly, and mail, and once a cake that a family had smuggled past the nurses with the solemnity of arms traffickers. Room 412 belonged to a man named Mr. Bergeron who had been there since before Simon started and who liked to argue. Simon brought him a newspaper every week because Mr. Bergeron claimed the television made his blood pressure rise, though he watched it for six hours a day regardless.

That Thursday, Mr. Bergeron had the newspaper folded to an article about the hospital buying a new machine, some scanner, the cost of which could apparently have funded the whole physiotherapy wing for a year. "Tell me," Mr. Bergeron said, pointing at it with a finger like a door hinge, "who decided that."

"I just deliver the newspaper," Simon said.

"Everybody just delivers something," said Mr. Bergeron. "That is the problem."

Simon did not have an answer, so he said the cake downstairs was going fast and left. In the elevator he thought about the debate club, where this exact fight had been running for two weeks now. Charles-Olivier had proposed the motion about the new gene-editing technology, the one the biology teacher kept calling "a clinical tool" in the tone of someone calling a wolf a large dog. Lilia was against it, mostly on the grounds that Charles-Olivier was for it, but she had also brought a real argument, something she had read in a philosophy book. Simon had been in the middle, which he told himself was nuance and which Lilia told him was cowardice with better branding.

The elevator stopped on two, where a nurse asked him to take a bag of bed linens to storage, and on three, where another nurse asked him why he was on three. He arrived back at the volunteer desk twenty minutes later carrying the linens he had originally been taking somewhere else, and Ms. Fortin, the volunteer coordinator, looked at him over her glasses the way one looks at weather.

"You missed the memo," she said, handing him a photocopied page. "We're short on Friday. You said you couldn't do Fridays."

"I said I couldn't do this Friday," Simon said, which was a lie he had told so smoothly he had half convinced himself, the way he had half convinced himself about the calculus test, and the week before that, and the week before that.

At the debate on Tuesday, Charles-Olivier opened with projections, curves rising on the projector like the necks of confident animals. Lilia stood up and said, "Before we talk about what this technology can do, somebody should say who speaks for the people who aren't born yet." She said she was quoting Hans Jonas, from 1979, a book called The Imperative of Responsibility, and she read the rule off an index card: "Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life." The room went quiet in the way rooms go quiet when someone has said something that no one can immediately improve on.

Charles-Olivier recovered first. "That's a nice sentence," he said. "It's also a sentence that would have blocked anesthesia, if you'd asked it early enough. Every intervention has trade-offs. Every intervention has unintended consequences. That's not a reason to freeze."

"It might be a reason to slow down," Lilia said.

Simon, who was supposed to be moderating, said nothing, and later wrote in his notes only the word "permanence," which he underlined twice for reasons he could not have explained to a teacher, and which looked, on the page, like a word belonging to someone more serious than he was.

On Thursday he found an envelope tucked inside Room 412's newspaper, with his name on it, misspelled. Inside was a note in blue ballpoint, the handwriting of a man writing on a clipboard against his knee. "To the newspaper boy," it began. "If you are the one who decides what comes into this room, then you have more power than the minister of health, who has never once brought me anything. Today you brought me a story about a machine. The machine will see inside people before they are sick. My son died of something it would have seen, eleven years ago, so do not tell me it is a waste of money. But the same money kept two nurses on my floor last spring, and one of them held my hand through a night I will not describe. I do not know which was right. Neither do you. You are seventeen or eighteen and you deliver flowers. But you are here, which is more than most, so I am telling you: the hard part is not choosing good over bad. It is choosing this good over that one, knowing you will never see the faces you helped and never see the faces you didn't." It was signed with a B and a line, as though the pen had run out or the writer had run out.

Simon read it in the corridor by the vending machines, which ate his toonie without dispensing anything, an event so consistent it had become almost comforting. He thought about the debate, and about the rule Lilia had read off the index card, and about how Mr. Bergeron's letter was not really about machines or nurses at all. It was about how a person stands in the present and tries to weigh a life against a life, one of which does not exist yet and one of which was in the bed down the hall wanting a newspaper.

He also thought, briefly and with the honesty he usually saved for two in the morning, that he was probably making the letter mean more than it meant, the way he had made the calculus test mean less than it meant. He was, he suspected, a synecdoche of something, one small part standing in for a generation that volunteered at hospitals to settle private accounts, and he was not sure that disqualified the volunteering. It might even be the trade-off nobody warns you about: the good you do for bad reasons still gets done, and the bad you avoid for good reasons still gets avoided, and the accounting between them is never going to balance.

On Friday he came in for the extra shift, telling Ms. Fortin his schedule had cleared up, which was technically the first fully true sentence he had said to her. He took the newspapers. Room 412 was empty, the bed stripped, the television off for the first time he could remember, and a housekeeper was folding the privacy curtain as though it had never been anything but fabric.

Simon stood in the doorway with the newspaper still under his arm.

"He left you this," the housekeeper said, and pointed to a Get Well Soon card propped on the windowsill, the kind sold in the gift shop, the kind that says everything and means it anyway.
